title: Aligned to what?
subtitle: A history of alignment, and how cultures have answered it
preface: Long before anyone built a computer, people told stories about made beings that served, misunderstood or turned on their makers. This book follows that worry from myth to the laboratories and laws of today, and asks a question the field rarely asks out loud: aligned to what? The world's traditions have answered it differently, and each answer has something to teach about a technology that may become more capable than the people who make it.

parts.title: Part one · The oldest alignment problems

chapters.title: The oldest alignment problems: myths of made beings
chapters.summary: Long before computers, stories from Greece to Guatemala imagined beings made rather than born and asked how such beings could be kept to their makers' purposes; this chapter retells the oldest of them.

paragraphs.text: The Stanford historian of science Adrienne Mayor argues in Gods and Robots (2018) that Greek myths imagined artificial life centuries before anyone could build it. The earliest example is in Homer's Iliad, where the smith-god Hephaestus is attended by handmaidens of gold. In A. T. Murray's translation they have understanding and speech. Mayor does not claim that the Greeks had robots. Her claim is that their stories had already asked what it would mean to share the world with things that act on their own, and whom such things would serve.

sources.title: Homer, Iliad 18.388-427, trans. A. T. Murray, Perseus Digital Library
sources.quote: handmaidens wrought of gold in the semblance of living maids. In them is understanding in their hearts, and in them speech

paragraphs.text: The same book of the Iliad gives Hephaestus tripods on golden wheels that roll to the gods' assembly and back 'at his wish'. These first imagined machines are aligned in the simplest way: they serve their maker and do nothing else. Mayor sees trouble begin when made beings leave the divine workshop. In a 2018 interview she said that when Talos and Pandora are sent to earth and meet humans, troubles follow. Centuries later Aristotle used the self-moving tripods for a thought experiment about labour: if tools worked by themselves, masters would need no slaves.

sources.title: Homer, Iliad 18.368ff, trans. A. T. Murray, Perseus Digital Library
sources.quote: golden wheels had he set beneath the base of each that of themselves they might enter the gathering of the gods at his wish

sources.title: Town Hall Seattle, interview with Adrienne Mayor (2018)
sources.quote: But when automatons like the bronze robot Talos and the artificial woman Pandora are sent to earth and interact with humans, then all kinds of troubles are unleashed.

sources.title: Aristotle, Politics 1.1253b, trans. H. Rackham, Perseus Digital Library
sources.quote: if thus shuttles wove and quills played harps of themselves, master-craftsmen would have no need of assistants and masters no need of slaves.

paragraphs.text: Talos was a bronze giant who guarded Crete for King Minos. In the ancient versions collected by the Theoi Project, he ran around the island three times a day and threw rocks at approaching ships. His life ran through a single vein closed by a stud at the ankle. The sorceress Medea undid him by promising immortality and then pulling out the stud, so that his ichor drained away. Mayor draws a broader lesson from his fate: no made guardian is final, because someone else can always surpass or destroy it.

sources.title: Theoi Project, Talos
sources.quote: she promised to make him immortal and then removed the stud, so that his ichor all flowed out and he expired.

sources.title: Palo Alto Online, 'Made, not born' (2019), on Adrienne Mayor
sources.quote: No matter what you build, someone else is going to be able to surpass it or destroy it.

paragraphs.text: Pandora is a darker case: a made being designed to harm the people she is sent to. In Hesiod's Works and Days, in Hugh Evelyn-White's translation, Zeus announces that he will give humans an evil thing as the price of stolen fire, and has Hephaestus mix earth and water to shape her while other gods add their gifts. The Theogony calls her a 'beautiful evil'. Mayor connects this to a pattern she sees across the myths, in which the most dangerous automata are commissioned by tyrants.

sources.title: Hesiod, Works and Days, trans. Evelyn-White, Theoi Project
sources.quote: But I will give men as the price for fire an evil thing in which they may all be glad of heart while they embrace their own destruction.

sources.title: Hesiod, Theogony, trans. Evelyn-White, Theoi Project
sources.quote: But when he had made the beautiful evil to be the price for the blessing, he brought her out

sources.title: Town Hall Seattle, interview with Adrienne Mayor (2018)
sources.quote: there was a strong link between autocratic rulers and machines of malice.

paragraphs.text: Not every classicist accepts this reading. Reviewing Gods and Robots for the Bryn Mawr Classical Review, Clara Bosak-Schroeder wrote that the book reopens rather than settles the question of how ancient magic relates to craft, and she worried that setting ancient devices beside modern ones overstates their likeness. A passage in Plato's Meno offers another ancient image of control. Socrates says the legendary statues of Daedalus run away unless they are fastened down. The safeguard there is not a better command but a tether.

sources.title: Clara Bosak-Schroeder, review of Gods and Robots, Bryn Mawr Classical Review 2019.08.09
sources.quote: I worry that the juxtapositions of ancient and modern material overdetermine Mayor’s claim that ancient devices are like modern ones.

sources.title: Plato, Meno 97d, trans. W. R. M. Lamb, Perseus Digital Library
sources.quote: That if they are not fastened up they play truant and run away; but, if fastened, they stay where they are.

paragraphs.text: Some of the oldest warnings concern a power that does exactly what it is asked. Midas is not a made being, but his story became a byword for this failure. In Ovid's Metamorphoses, in Brookes More's translation, the god Bacchus offers Midas any reward, and Midas asks that whatever he touches turn to gold. The god grants the wish while grieving that Midas chose harm, and does nothing to correct it. In 2016 the computer scientist Stuart Russell called the danger of an AI pursuing a badly stated objective 'the old King Midas problem'.

sources.title: Ovid, Metamorphoses 11, trans. Brookes More, Perseus Digital Library
sources.quote: Bacchus agreed to his unfortunate request, with grief that Midas chose for harm and not for good.

sources.title: Future of Life Institute, interview with Stuart Russell (2016)
sources.quote: It’s the old King Midas problem.

paragraphs.text: The tale now known as the sorcerer's apprentice is far older than Goethe. The folklorist D. L. Ashliman of the University of Pittsburgh classifies it as tale type 325* and traces it to Lucian's satire The Lover of Lies, from the second century CE. In the Fowlers' translation, a man overhears the spell that makes a pestle fetch water but not the word that stops it. When he splits the pestle with an axe, both halves carry on. Ashliman notes that Lucian told the story to mock belief in such wonders.

sources.title: Lucian, The Lover of Lies, trans. H. W. and F. G. Fowler, ToposText
sources.quote: I took an axe, and cut the pestle in two. The result was that both halves took pitchers and fetched water

sources.title: D. L. Ashliman, The Sorcerer's Apprentice: folktales of type 325*, University of Pittsburgh
sources.quote: His purpose in The Lover of Lies was to belittle belief in supernatural tales of the type presented here.

paragraphs.text: Goethe's ballad Der Zauberlehrling, written in 1797, gave the story its modern form. While his master is away, the apprentice orders an old broom, addressed as a long-time servant, to carry water. Then he realises he has forgotten the word that stops it. Splitting the broom doubles the flood. Only the returning master can send the spirits back, and the ballad closes by saying that the old master calls them up only for his own purpose. Control here lies in knowing the whole command, including how to stop, and in keeping that knowledge with someone competent.

sources.title: Goethe, Der Zauberlehrling (1798 printing), German Wikisource
sources.quote: Hab ich doch das Wort vergessen!

sources.title: Goethe, Der Zauberlehrling, closing lines, German Wikisource
sources.quote: Denn als Geister Ruft euch nur zu seinem Zwecke, Erst hervor der alte Meister.

paragraphs.text: The Thousand and One Nights adds a different twist: a servant whose loyalty drifts. In Edward William Lane's translation of the story of the fisherman, a jinni whom Solomon sealed in a bottle vows during his first century of captivity to make his liberator rich forever. As the centuries pass his vows change, and at last he swears to kill whoever frees him. When a poor fisherman opens the bottle, the jinni says he will kill him for that very reason. The fisherman survives by wit rather than force, tricking the jinni back inside.

sources.title: The Story of the Fisherman, trans. Edward William Lane, Hivemind (Georgia Tech)
sources.quote: There I remained a hundred years; and I said in my heart, Whosoever shall liberate me, I will enrich him for ever

sources.title: The Story of the Fisherman, trans. Lane
sources.quote: I am not going to kill thee but for that very reason, because thou hast liberated me.

paragraphs.text: The genie of the lamp, now the best-known wish-granter, is a late arrival. Research by Paulo Lemos Horta, reported by the Brazilian news agency ANBA, points to the Aleppine storyteller Hanna Diyab, from whom the French translator Antoine Galland recorded hearing the story. In the English version on Project Gutenberg, the genie is the slave of whoever holds the lamp, so a thief who steals it can command it. The literary scholar Marina Warner describes the jinn's position in one phrase: to hear is to obey.

sources.title: ANBA, 'The original Aladdin came from Aleppo, Syria' (2019)
sources.quote: In the same lines, in his journal, Galland mentioned having heard the story of Aladdin from Diyab.

sources.title: The Arabian Nights Entertainments (1914), Project Gutenberg 19860, PGLAF mirror
sources.quote: I am ready to obey thee as thy slave, and the slave of all those who have that lamp in their hands; I, and the other slaves of the lamp.

sources.title: Marina Warner, 'Of Shimmering Flame' (Szeged University Press, 2025)
sources.quote: entirely subject to whomsoever chance places in that role: to hear is to obey is the jinns’ watchword.

sections.heading: Clay, letters and the word for truth

paragraphs.text: Jewish tradition supplies the most influential story of a made servant. A short passage in the Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 65b, says that the sage Rava created a man and sent him to Rabbi Zeira. In the English translation on Sefaria, Zeira spoke to the man and received no reply. From the creature's silence Zeira concluded that it had been made by one of the sages, and told it to return to its dust. The test of the made being is speech, and the remedy is unmaking.

sources.title: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 65b, William Davidson edition (Sefaria API)
sources.quote: Rabbi Zeira would speak to him but he would not reply.

sources.title: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 65b (Sefaria API)
sources.quote: one of the Sages. Return to your dust.

paragraphs.text: The historian of Kabbalah Gershom Scholem traced how medieval mystics linked golem-making to combinations of letters and to the Hebrew word emet, truth. In one tale he retells, the prophet Jeremiah and his son make a man with 'truth' written on his forehead. The creature erases the first letter, leaving met, 'dead', to warn its makers that their act edges toward blasphemy. Scholem defined the golem as a creature controlled by its maker that may also tend to outgrow that control.

sources.title: Gershom Scholem, 'The Golem of Prague & The Golem of Rehovoth', Commentary (Wayback Machine copy)
sources.quote: But this newly created man had a knife in his hand, with which he erased the letter aleph from the word emeth (“truth”); there remained the word meth (“dead”).

sources.title: Scholem, 'The Golem of Prague & The Golem of Rehovoth'
sources.quote: which is controlled by its creator and performs tasks set by him, but which at the same time may have a dangerous tendency to outgrow that control

paragraphs.text: The famous golem of Prague is younger than it looks. Curt Leviant, writing for the National Endowment for the Humanities, notes that the legend of Rabbi Judah Loew's golem first appears in the early nineteenth century and that neither Loew's works nor those of his contemporaries mention it. It spread through Yudl Rosenberg's 1909 book, which Rosenberg passed off as an old manuscript. In Scholem's retelling, the rabbi removed the slip bearing the Name of God each Sabbath so that the golem rested; one week he forgot, and it ran amok. The off switch depended on a ritual habit.

sources.title: Curt Leviant, 'Golem Revival', HUMANITIES (National Endowment for the Humanities), 2008
sources.quote: makes its debut in the first third of the nineteenth century. None of the Maharal’s works nor those of his contemporaries mentions the golem legend

sources.title: Scholem, 'The Golem of Prague & The Golem of Rehovoth'
sources.quote: Every Sabbath the Rabbi would remove the slip of paper with the Name of God on it, and the Golem would become inanimate for the day

paragraphs.text: Court stories elsewhere imagined made beings as gifts to rulers. The Liezi, a Daoist text compiled around the fourth century CE, tells of an artificer named Yan Shi who presents King Mu of Zhou with a singing, dancing figure. In Lionel Giles's 1912 translation the automaton flirts with the ladies of the court, and the furious king orders its maker's death, until Yan Shi takes it apart to show it is only leather, wood, glue and paint. The king then asks whether human skill can match the work of what the Chinese text calls the maker of transformations.

sources.title: Lionel Giles (trans.), Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzu, Book 5, Wikisource
sources.quote: the automaton winked his eye and made sundry advances to the ladies in attendance on the King

sources.title: Liezi, Tang Wen chapter (Chinese text), Chinese Wikisource
sources.quote: 人之巧乃可與造化者同功乎

paragraphs.text: A Buddhist legend preserved in the Lokapannatti imagines machines on guard duty. In Mayor's retelling for The Conversation, King Ajatasatru set 'spirit movement machines' to guard the Buddha's relics until a foretold king would distribute them; Asoka later fought them and ended up commanding them. The craft is said to come from robot makers in the West, who were forbidden to reveal their secrets on pain of being hunted by robotic assassins. Mayor acknowledges that most scholars date the story to medieval times, and argues that it could be much older.

sources.title: Adrienne Mayor, 'Robots guarded Buddha's relics in a legend of ancient India', The Conversation (2019)
sources.quote: Robot makers were forbidden to leave or reveal their secrets – if they did, robotic assassins pursued and killed them.

sources.title: Mayor, The Conversation (2019)
sources.quote: Most scholars assume it arose in medieval Islamic and European times. But I think the story could be much older.

paragraphs.text: Indian treatises also describe mechanical servants. The Samarangana Sutradhara, an eleventh-century architectural text attributed to King Bhoja of Dhar, though his authorship is uncertain, describes mechanical figures for palaces, including dolls that refilled oil lamps and danced; its author declines to explain how to build some machines, citing secrecy. The scholar of religion Signe Cohen, in I, Yantra (2024), translates many Hindu, Buddhist and Jain robot tales into English for the first time and argues that they show how their authors thought about the nature of humanity.

sources.title: Samarangana Sutradhara (Wikipedia, basic facts only)
sources.quote: male and female dolls that refilled oil lamps, danced, played instruments, and re-enacted scenes from Hindu mythology

sources.title: SUNY Press, Signe Cohen, I, Yantra (2024)
sources.quote: ancient yantra (robot) tales reveal how their Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain authors thought about the nature of humanity

paragraphs.text: At the Artuqid court of Diyarbakir around 1206, the engineer Ismail al-Jazari described automata built to stand in for servants. The Public Domain Review, presenting a later copy of his Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices, describes a figure of a standing slave who serves the king wine, and a washing device made for a king who disliked being served by human attendants. The Review's editors draw a comparison with today: like our AI assistants, they write, al-Jazari's inventions never rise above the role of an indentured labourer.

sources.title: Public Domain Review, 'Manuscript of Ismail al-Jazari's Ingenious Mechanical Devices'
sources.quote: a standing slave holding a fish and a goblet from which he serves wine to the king

sources.title: Public Domain Review, on al-Jazari
sources.quote: Not unlike our “AI assistants”, al-Jazarī’s inventions are never allowed to transcend the category of indentured laborer

paragraphs.text: In Edo-period Japan, mechanical dolls called karakuri performed similar small services. The Kyoto University Museum describes a tea-serving doll whose mechanism was published in 1796 in Hosokawa Hanzō's Karakuri zui. When the master places a cup on its tray, the doll advances toward the guest, stops while the guest drinks, and returns. Its obedience is built into the mechanism itself: the doll serves because of how it is made, and only the master's gesture sets it going.

sources.title: Kyoto University Museum, 'Mechanisms of KARAKURI dolls'
sources.quote: If a master puts a tea cup on the tray which the doll supports, the doll will begin to advance

sources.title: Nippon.com, 'The Dolls that Sparked Japan's Love of Robots' (2012)
sources.quote: Many of those secrets were revealed in 1796 when Hosokawa Hanzō, better known as “Karakuri Hanzō,” published his book Karakuri zui

paragraphs.text: The K'iche' Maya Popol Vuh, written down in alphabetic K'iche' between 1554 and 1558, tells of creator gods who try several times to make beings that will remember and honour them. In Allen J. Christenson's translation, the first being, of mud, speaks without knowledge and dissolves. The second, carved of wood, looks and speaks like people and multiplies, but does not remember its makers. Christenson notes that the early creations fail chiefly because they cannot worship the gods in intelligible speech. Alignment, in this text, is a relationship of remembrance and address.

sources.title: Allen J. Christenson, Popol Vuh (Mesoweb edition)
sources.quote: They did not remember their Framer or their Shaper.

sources.title: Christenson, Popol Vuh, note 88
sources.quote: The principal reason for the downfall of the first created beings was their inability to communicate in human speech, so the gods could not be worshiped with intelligible words.

paragraphs.text: The wooden people end in a revolt of their own possessions. Their dogs, turkeys, grinding stones, griddles and pots rise against them, each naming its injury. The animals say that the wooden people caused them pain and ate them, and now will be eaten in turn; the pots complain of being thrown on the fire. Christenson reads the dogs' complaint as a judgment on masters whose only speech to them was beatings. The story places the cause of revolt in mistreatment, not in the nature of the tools.

sources.title: Christenson, Popol Vuh
sources.quote: Our mouths and our faces are sooty. You were forever throwing us upon the fire and burning us.

sources.title: Christenson, Popol Vuh, commentary
sources.quote: The dogs are pointing out that, instead, their speech has been limited to beatings and violence.

paragraphs.text: When the gods finally succeed, with people made of maize, they face the opposite problem. The new beings see and know everything and give thanks, but the gods worry that the people's works will equal their own. So they cloud the people's sight, which the text likens to breath on the face of a mirror. Christenson's note states the purpose plainly: the gods limited the first people's vision. The makers keep their creation aligned by restricting what it can do.

sources.title: Christenson, Popol Vuh
sources.quote: Their works will merely be equated with ours.

sources.title: Christenson, Popol Vuh, note 493
sources.quote: Thus the gods clouded the eyes of the first men so that their vision would be limited.

paragraphs.text: Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818) turns the question around and asks what a maker owes the made. Victor Frankenstein imagines that a new species would bless him as its creator, then flees the creature in disgust the moment it wakes. When they meet again, the creature offers a bargain: obedience to his 'natural lord and king' if Victor will perform his own part. He traces his crimes to neglect, saying that misery made him a fiend. Victor later destroys the half-made companion, fearing that the pair could found a race of devils.

sources.title: Mary Shelley, Frankenstein (1818), Project Gutenberg 84, PGLAF mirror
sources.quote: I am thy creature, and I will be even mild and docile to my natural lord and king if thou wilt also perform thy part, the which thou owest me.

sources.title: Frankenstein (1818)
sources.quote: I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend. Make me happy, and I shall again be virtuous.

paragraphs.text: Karel Čapek's play R.U.R. (1920) gave the world the word 'robot'. The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction notes that it comes from the Czech robota, statute labour, and reads the play as a comment on slavery; Čapek credited the word to his brother Josef. In the 1923 English version on Project Gutenberg, the factory's founder simplified the human being into a worker with minimal needs. The owners promise freedom from toil, a sceptic predicts that every worker will be unemployed, and the Robots finally rise and destroy humanity.

sources.title: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, 'Robots'
sources.quote: derived from the Czech robota (statute labour), making it clear that Čapek intended his drama to comment on Slavery

sources.title: Blackbird (Virginia Commonwealth University), Karel Čapek's 1933 note on the word robot
