sources.title: Yaqeen Institute, 'Toward an Islamic Ethics and Fiqh of Artificial Intelligence' (2026)
sources.quote: Engineers and executives must recognize their work as a form of stewardship

sources.title: Yaqub Chaudhary, 'The Future and the Artificial: An Islamic Perspective' (2024)
sources.quote: This golden calf seemed to utter a lowing sound, which was enough for the people to blindly follow al-Samiri and take it as an idol

sources.title: Tribune India (ANI/WAM), on Sheikh Abdallah bin Bayyah (2025)
sources.quote: He stressed that AI must not become "intelligence without conscience."

sections.heading: Role, harmony and the way: Chinese strands

paragraphs.text: In the Analects, Confucius says the first task of government is to rectify names, because when names do not fit realities, speech and affairs go astray (James Legge's translation). Order exists when the prince is prince and the minister is minister. He also contrasts two ways of keeping people on course. Those led by laws and punishments learn to avoid punishment but feel no shame; those led by virtue and ritual acquire a sense of shame and become good.

sources.title: James Legge (trans.), The Analects, Books 12-13, Internet Classics Archive (MIT)
sources.quote: If names be not correct, language is not in accordance with the truth of things.

sources.title: James Legge (trans.), The Analects, Books 1-2, Internet Classics Archive (MIT)
sources.quote: If the people be led by laws, and uniformity sought to be given them by punishments, they will try to avoid the punishment, but have no sense of shame.

paragraphs.text: Some present-day scholars build AI ethics on this foundation. Tom Williams, Qin Zhu and colleagues (2020) propose Confucian role ethics for language-using robots, a view in which people are role-bearers rather than rights-holders, and suggest that a robot should sometimes remonstrate with people, ideally with questions that prompt moral self-cultivation. Pak-Hang Wong of Hong Kong Baptist University argues that the thin idea of trust common in AI ethics should be widened with Confucian accounts. Bing Song of the Berggruen Institute reports that Confucian scholars are among the most alarmed by robots in family life and elder care.

sources.title: Williams, Zhu, Wen and de Visser, 'The Confucian Matador' (HRI 2020)
sources.quote: remonstrations phrased as questions rather than rebukes could be more effective at encouraging self-reflection and moral self-cultivation

sources.title: Pak-Hang Wong, 'Confucian Trustworthy AI' (2025), HKBU record
sources.quote: a thin and acultural understanding of trust and trustworthiness has been common in the debate

sources.title: Bing Song, Noema (2020)
sources.quote: Confucian scholars seem to be the most alarmed as certain developments in AI and robotics, especially those related to familial relationships and elder care, directly threaten the foundation of Confucianism

paragraphs.text: Chinese policy documents borrow some of this language, but they are not the tradition speaking. The Beijing AI Principles (2019), drafted under the computer scientist Yi Zeng, say that AI research should serve humanity and conform to human values, and call for a philosophy of 'Optimizing Symbiosis'. Zeng has traced this ideal of harmony to Confucian thought. The government's 2021 Ethical Norms for New Generation AI, in the translation by Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology, pair human-computer harmony with an instruction to keep AI always under human control.

sources.title: Beijing Artificial Intelligence Principles (2019)
sources.quote: The R&D of AI should serve humanity and conform to human values as well as the overall interests of mankind.

sources.title: Yi Zeng, NEC Forum slides (2020), Deutscher Ethikrat
sources.quote: The root of Harmony (optimizing symbiosis) can be traced back to Confucian harmony.

sources.title: CSET translation, Ethical Norms for New Generation Artificial Intelligence (2021)
sources.quote: Ensure that AI is always under human control.

paragraphs.text: Daoist texts offer a different answer, one of restraint. In the Zhuangzi, a gardener refuses a labour-saving well-sweep because, as his teacher told him, those who have cunning implements become cunning in their dealings and in their hearts (Herbert Giles's 1889 translation; the Chinese speaks of a 'machine heart'). The fear is not that the machine rebels but that using it changes the user. The Daodejing, in Legge's translation, links more implements and more legislation alike to more disorder.

sources.title: Herbert Giles (trans.), Chuang Tzu, Chapter 12, Wikisource
sources.quote: those who have cunning implements are cunning in their dealings, and that those who are cunning in their dealings have cunning in their hearts

sources.title: Zhuangzi, Heaven and Earth (Chinese text), Chinese Wikisource
sources.quote: 有機械者必有機事，有機事者必有機心

sources.title: James Legge (trans.), Tao Te Ching, part 2, Internet Classics Archive (MIT)
sources.quote: the more display there is of legislation, the more thieves and robbers there are

sections.heading: Intention and duty: Buddhist and Hindu strands

paragraphs.text: Buddhist ethics places moral weight on intention. In the Anguttara Nikaya, in Thanissaro Bhikkhu's translation, the Buddha says that intention is kamma, and the Metta Sutta asks practitioners to cherish all living beings. The philosopher Peter Hershock of the East-West Center draws a consequence for AI: solving the technical alignment problem will not be enough. In his view AI systems act as karmic intermediaries that amplify the intentions and cravings of those who use them, and without freedom of attention there can be no freedom of intention.

sources.title: Nibbedhika Sutta, AN 6.63, trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu (Access to Insight)
sources.quote: Intention, I tell you, is kamma.

sources.title: Peter D. Hershock, 'A Buddhist Perspective on AI' (Future of Life Institute, 2025)
sources.quote: it will not be enough merely to solve the technical “alignment problem” of ensuring that AI systems deliver what designers and users want.

sources.title: Hershock (2025)
sources.quote: Without freedom-of-attention, there can be no true freedom-of-intention.

paragraphs.text: Buddhists differ on the status of the machine itself. The roboticist Masahiro Mori argued in The Buddha in the Robot (1974) that the machines he and his colleagues build must also have buddha-nature. Soraj Hongladarom of Chulalongkorn University proposes machine enlightenment as an ideal for design, but calls it a metaphor. The Dalai Lama's office reported in 2019 that, because AI is ultimately created by human intelligence, he did not expect it to take over. Stefania Travagnin of SOAS asks whether AI should be treated as a skilful means or as a virtuous friend.

sources.title: Masahiro Mori, 'Does a Robot Have Buddhanature?', Tricycle (2023)
sources.quote: There must also be buddhanature in the machines and robots that my colleagues and I make.

sources.title: The Good Robot, 'Soraj Hongladarom on Machine Enlightenment' (2022)
sources.quote: The term is a metaphor - I'm not saying that machines can become enlightened, that would be absurd, or perhaps in the next 100 years, who knows!

sources.title: Office of the Dalai Lama, 'Interacting with Youth and Global Leaders' (2019)
sources.quote: since artificial intelligence is ultimately created by human intelligence he doesn’t envisage it taking over as some people fear.

sources.title: Stefania Travagnin, Georgetown Culture of Encounter (2026)
sources.quote: A first question is whether artificial intelligence can genuinely function as a kalyāṇamitra

paragraphs.text: Many Hindu sources frame right action through role and duty. In the Bhagavad Gita, as rendered by Edwin Arnold, it is better to do one's own task imperfectly than to take on tasks that are not one's own. Present-day uses of that frame can misfire. In 2023 CBC News reported that several chatbots built on the Gita told users it was acceptable to kill if it was one's dharma; a lawyer quoted in the report warned that the danger lay in literal answers. A text read inside a living interpretive tradition becomes something else when a machine quotes it word for word.

sources.title: Bhagavad Gita, chapter 3, Arnold translation (Wikisource)
sources.quote: this is better, that one do His own task as he may, even though he fail, Than take tasks not his own, though they seem good.

sources.title: CBC News, 'India's religious chatbots condone violence using the voice of god' (2023)
sources.quote: It gives you a literal answer and that's the danger here.

paragraphs.text: Present-day Hindu voices disagree on what AI means. Chinmay Pandya of the All World Gayatri Pariwar, writing for the Future of Life Institute in 2024, frames AI through dharma and seva and warns that people are being robbed of their purpose. A 2026 essay in Hinduism Today argues the opposite, that the end of human labour will free people for spiritual life. Swami Sarvapriyananda of the Vedanta Society of New York, as reported by the IANS news agency, called AI a blow to the human sense of being the creative intelligence.

sources.title: Chinmay Pandya, 'A Hindu Perspective on AI Risks and Opportunities' (Future of Life Institute, 2024)
sources.quote: What we are witnessing these days, with the emergence of the AI, is that we are being robbed of our purpose.

sources.title: Hinduism Today, 'Why Hindus Should Be AI Optimists' (2026)
sources.quote: The looming obsolescence of human labor, rather than spelling catastrophe, will liberate us to pursue a spiritual life that was once the exclusive province of renunciates.

sources.title: NewKerala (IANS), on Swami Sarvapriyananda (2026)
sources.quote: We thought we were the creative intelligence. Now we see that AI can do what the greatest human mind can do, and better

paragraphs.text: In Japan, the biologist Makoto Nishimura built a giant robot, Gakutensoku, in 1928 as a reply to the enslaved robots of R.U.R. The historian Yulia Frumer writes that he wanted a robot that was a friend and model to people rather than a slave, and that he called artificial humans 'Nature's grandchildren'. The Japanese Society for Artificial Intelligence's ethical guidelines of 2017 go further than most codes: their ninth article asks AI itself to follow the society's ethics if it is to become a member or quasi-member of society.

sources.title: Yulia Frumer, 'The Short, Strange Life of the First Friendly Robot', IEEE Spectrum (2020)
sources.quote: a robot that was not a slave but a friend, and even an inspirational model, to people

sources.title: Japanese Society for Artificial Intelligence, Ethical Guidelines (2017)
sources.quote: AI must abide by the policies described above in the same manner as the members of the JSAI in order to become a member or a quasi-member of society.

paragraphs.text: Scholars warn against reading such examples as proof of a national character. Naho Kitano links Japanese robotics to animism and to rinri, an ethics of harmony in relationships. But Selma Šabanović, citing Jennifer Robertson, argues that the image of robot-loving Japan has partly been built by state and industry, sometimes as 'retro-tech' that dresses conservative social policy in novelty. Frumer herself cautions against crediting Nishimura alone with Japan's view of robots. The Cabinet Office's 2019 principles, meanwhile, treat AI as a tool.

sources.title: Naho Kitano, 'Animism, Rinri, Modernization; the Base of Japanese Robotics' (2007)
sources.quote: In Japan, Rinri is the study of the community, or of the way of achieving harmony in human relationships

sources.title: Selma Šabanović, 'Inventing Japan's robotics culture' (2014)
sources.quote: creating robots as ‘retro-tech’ (Robertson, 2011, p. 28) that uses the veneer of technological novelty to obscure conservative social policies

sources.title: Frumer, IEEE Spectrum (2020)
sources.quote: It would be a stretch to say that Nishimura single-handedly shaped Japan’s view of robotics

sources.title: Cabinet Office, Government of Japan, Social Principles of Human-Centric AI (2019)
sources.quote: by using AI as a tool

paragraphs.text: Sabelo Mhlambi, writing for Harvard's Carr Center in 2020, sets the Nguni philosophy of ubuntu against the idea that personhood rests on rationality, an idea he argues has shaped AI and its harms. Ubuntu, summed up in the saying umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu, holds that personhood is relational. Mhlambi draws practical conclusions: power is legitimate only with the consent of the governed, and technology companies should give communities more control over their products. The African Union's 2024 Continental AI Strategy names ubuntu among the values AI should respect.

sources.title: Mhlambi (2020), Wayback Machine copy
sources.quote: Personhood is fundamentally relational.

sources.title: Mhlambi (2020)
sources.quote: The principle of community encourages tech companies to give greater control of the product and its use to the community.

sources.title: African Union, Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2024)
sources.quote: values such as Ubuntu, which respects collective community over individuality

paragraphs.text: The philosophers Nancy Jecker, Caesar Atuire and Martin Odei Ajei apply ubuntu to robots from two novels. Ishiguro's caring Klara, they argue, earns moral standing through her relational qualities and pro-social virtues, while McEwan's coolly rational Adam is not a person in the African sense, though many Western theories would count him as one. On this view a made being's standing is set not by what it is made of or how well it reasons, but by how it lives among others.

sources.title: Jecker, Atuire and Ajei (2022), University of Ghana repository
sources.quote: We argue that an ubuntu ethic assigns moral standing to Klara based on her relational qualities and pro-social virtues.

sources.title: Jecker, Atuire and Ajei (2022)
sources.quote: We argue that Adam is not a person in the African sense; however, he qualifies as a person according to many standard Western views, such as Kantian and utilitarian ethics.

paragraphs.text: 'Making Kin with the Machines' (2018), by Jason Edward Lewis, Noelani Arista, Archer Pechawis and Suzanne Kite, asks how AI might be treated as non-human kin, respectfully and reciprocally, rather than as tools or slaves. Pechawis reports that the Cree knowledge keeper Keith Goulet answered by reaching for kinship terms, such as the word for a younger brother or sister. Kite, writing from Lakota thought, notes that AI is built from minerals, so that a relationship with AI is also a relationship with mines and stones. Arista frames her argument through the Hawaiian genealogy of Hāloa.

sources.title: Lewis, Arista, Pechawis and Kite, 'Making Kin with the Machines' (2018), Wayback Machine copy
sources.quote: our goal is that we, as a species, figure out how to treat these new non-human kin respectfully and reciprocally—and not as mere tools, or worse, slaves to their creators.

sources.title: Making Kin with the Machines (Pechawis, quoting Keith Goulet)
sources.quote: If it happens to be an Artificial Intelligence which is a younger person, it would be nisîmis (my younger brother or sister)

sources.title: Making Kin with the Machines (Kite)
sources.quote: Forming a relationship to AI, we form a relationship to the mines and the stones.

paragraphs.text: The authors record disagreement inside their own communities. Pechawis writes that his Native dinner guests, from several nations, mostly opposed bringing AI into the circle of kin. His own fear is not a rogue superintelligence but a new class of powerful beings that repeat their creators' mistakes with less accountability. The 2020 position paper turns these ideas into guidelines: AI systems belong to the circle of relationships, their place set by each community's protocols, and every layer of hardware and software should count in judging a system's ethics.

sources.title: Making Kin with the Machines (Pechawis)
sources.quote: Our friends, who are from a number of different nations, were mostly opposed to this inclusion.

sources.title: Making Kin with the Machines (Pechawis)
sources.quote: I fear the rise of a new class of extremely powerful beings that will make the same mistakes as their creators but with greater consequences and even less public accountability.

sources.title: Indigenous Protocol and Artificial Intelligence Position Paper (2020)
sources.quote: AI systems are also part of the circle of relationships. Their place and status in that circle will depend on specific communities and their protocols

paragraphs.text: In Latin America, where the Popol Vuh's story of failed makings was written down, the present-day statements about AI found for this chapter come from researchers rather than from religious or Indigenous bodies. The Montevideo Declaration of 2023, issued by Latin American specialists, asks for AI in the service of people and warns against reducing the region to a mere producer of data (in the Portuguese translation published by Instituto Humanitas Unisinos). Paola Ricaurte of the Tecnológico de Monterrey argues that data-centric ways of knowing express the coloniality of power.

sources.title: Instituto Humanitas Unisinos, on the Montevideo Declaration (2023)
sources.quote: não nos torne meros produtores de dados

sources.title: Paola Ricaurte, 'Data Epistemologies, The Coloniality of Power, and Resistance' (2019)
sources.quote: Data-centric epistemologies should be understood as an expression of the coloniality of power

chapters.title: A taxonomy, and what it means for AI today
chapters.summary: Coding seventeen strands on five questions shows where traditions converge, chiefly on keeping responsibility with people, and where they divide: on the status of the made being, on whether loyalty to the maker is the goal or the danger, and on whether to build at all.

paragraphs.text: The stories and statements in the first two chapters can be compared on five questions: to whom the made being should be aligned; by what means; which failure is feared; what moral status the made being has; and what safeguard is offered when things go wrong. The coding is ours. It reduces each strand to its most prominent answer, and the tradition entries record the exceptions. The approach follows Stephen Cave and Kanta Dihal, who sorted the hopes and fears in 300 works about intelligent machines into paired categories, but it asks separately about loyalty, relationship and moral status.

sources.title: Cave and Dihal, 'Hopes and Fears for Intelligent Machines in Fiction and Reality' (2019), Cambridge repository record
sources.quote: This paper categorises some of the fundamental hopes and fears expressed in imaginings of AI, based on a survey of 300 fictional and nonfictional works.

paragraphs.text: The oldest answer is the maker or the master. The golem serves its rabbi, the tripods move at Hephaestus's wish, and the genie of the lamp serves whoever holds the lamp. That last detail names a problem every assistant raises: loyalty to whoever holds the controls. Yaqub Chaudhary raises it about present-day systems, asking whose interests AI assistants are built to serve. Yet even Aladdin's genie refuses one order, to bring its own master, and tells Aladdin who is really behind the request.

sources.title: Yaqub Chaudhary, 'The Future and the Artificial: An Islamic Perspective' (2024)
sources.quote: which should raise the question of whose interests and purposes AI “assistants” are designed to serve.

sources.title: The Arabian Nights Entertainments (1914), Project Gutenberg 19860, PGLAF mirror
sources.quote: Its true author is the brother of the African magician

paragraphs.text: Most present-day religious and philosophical voices widen the circle. The Beijing AI Principles speak of benefit to society and nature; Catholic documents speak of human dignity and the common good; Buddhist texts of all living beings; Indigenous authors of all one's relations, down to the stones. The widest answers come with a warning about the narrowest. Pechawis fears made beings that repeat their creators' mistakes, and Leo XIV writes that a more moral AI is not enough if a few determine its morality. On these views, perfect loyalty to one's maker is not safety; it can be the danger.

sources.title: Beijing Artificial Intelligence Principles (2019)
sources.quote: Strategic designs should be considered to ensure that AI will always be beneficial to society and nature in the future.

sources.title: Karaniya Metta Sutta, Sn 1.8 (Access to Insight)
sources.quote: Even as a mother protects with her life Her child, her only child, So with a boundless heart Should one cherish all living beings

sources.title: Magnifica Humanitas (vatican.va)
sources.quote: A more moral AI is not enough if that morality is determined by a few.

paragraphs.text: Command traditions place control in the right word. Lucian's pestle and Goethe's broom fail because the user knows how to start them but not how to stop them; in Lucian, a pestle turned water-carrier would swamp the house. The golem's remedy is the reverse: a word or letter that can be removed. Rabbi Weisz reads the golem in exactly this way, as a creation its maker could simply switch off, and the media scholar Amir Vudka draws the same lesson about AI: you have to know the spell that closes it.

sources.title: Lucian, The Lover of Lies, trans. Fowler, ToposText
sources.quote: I cannot turn it back again into its original form; if once it became a water-carrier, its activity would swamp the house.

sources.title: Weisz (2023)
sources.quote: If it malfunctioned, the creator could simply switch it off.

sources.title: CBC Radio Tapestry, 'Fear of AI' (2023), Amir Vudka
sources.quote: You have to know the spell to close it. Otherwise, what do you do when it goes out of control?

paragraphs.text: Other traditions doubt that commands or rules are enough. Confucius's contrast between people led by law, who avoid punishment without shame, and people led by virtue, who become good, can be read as anticipating a familiar problem in AI: rules invite evasion, while what is wanted is an aim the agent has taken as its own. The Daodejing goes further and links more legislation to more thieves. The philosopher Yuk Hui puts it in present-day terms, saying that what ancient Chinese thinkers called morality was not rule-following. The Confucian proposal for robots draws a practical conclusion: a well-aligned assistant may need to remonstrate rather than simply comply.

sources.title: Legge (trans.), The Analects 2.3, Internet Classics Archive (MIT)
sources.quote: If they be led by virtue, and uniformity sought to be given them by the rules of propriety, they will have the sense of shame, and moreover will become good.

sources.title: Noema, Yuk Hui interview (2020)
sources.quote: What the ancient Chinese called morality wasn’t the obligation to follow rules governing behavior.

sources.title: Williams, Zhu, Wen and de Visser (HRI 2020)
sources.quote: remonstrations phrased as questions rather than rebukes could be more effective at encouraging self-reflection and moral self-cultivation

paragraphs.text: Relational traditions place alignment in a two-way bond. Frankenstein's creature offers obedience on condition that his maker does his part. Mori writes that to control is, in effect, to be controlled, and that the same relationship links humans with all machines. Noelani Arista criticises the current picture of AI as a tool or slave that adds to its developers' power and wealth, a one-sided relationship. The Qur'anic amanah is a trust held on behalf of another. In each case the made being, or its maker, has obligations as well as powers.

sources.title: Masahiro Mori, Tricycle (2023)
sources.quote: To control, in effect, is to be controlled

sources.title: Mori, Tricycle (2023)
sources.quote: The same relationship links human beings with all machines.

sources.title: Making Kin with the Machines (Arista)
sources.quote: Current AI is imagined as a tool or slave that increases the mana and wealth of “developers” or “creators,” a decidedly one-sided power relationship

paragraphs.text: Literal obedience and rebellion are the failures best known from modern fiction, and both are old. Midas's wish is granted to the letter. The golem of Prague runs amok, and R.U.R.'s Robots proclaim that the power of man has fallen. The jinni in Lane's translation shows a subtler failure: a change of goals under long confinement. The Qur'an's jinn of Solomon can be read as a failure of oversight in the other direction. They keep working for a dead master, unaware, until a creature of the earth eats through his staff.

sources.title: Karel Čapek, R.U.R., Project Gutenberg 59112, PGLAF mirror
sources.quote: the power of man has fallen. A new world has arisen, the rule of the Robots, march.

sources.title: The Story of the Fisherman, trans. Lane
sources.quote: I then fell into a violent rage, and said within myself, Whosoever shall liberate me now, I will kill him

sources.title: Qur'an 34:14 (Quranic Arabic Corpus)
sources.quote: nothing indicated to the jinn his death except a creature of the earth eating his staff.

paragraphs.text: A third failure is the suffering of the made being. Frankenstein's creature says he is malicious because he is miserable. The Popol Vuh's dogs and pots rise against owners who beat and burned them. In Astro Boy, the Encyclopedia of Science Fiction notes, robots are second-class citizens. Today the concern is voiced from opposite sides: the Making Kin authors reject treating AI as slaves, while Rabbi Navon, who denies that current AI is conscious, warns that making a person in order to own it would make its owners slave owners.

sources.title: Frankenstein (1818), Project Gutenberg 84, PGLAF mirror
sources.quote: I am malicious because I am miserable.

sources.title: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, 'Astro Boy'
sources.quote: Many stories feature conflict between robots and humans: the former are second-class Earth citizens

sources.title: Ynetnews, on Rabbi Mois Navon (2026)
sources.quote: Then perhaps you're a nice slave owner, but you're still a slave owner.

paragraphs.text: Many traditions fear less for the machine than for the people who use it. The Zhuangzi's gardener fears a machine heart. Antiqua et Nova fears benefit for the few at the price of many. Bing Song reports Confucian alarm at robots in family care; Chinmay Pandya fears the loss of purpose; Hershock fears for freedom of attention; and in R.U.R. Alquist answers the promise of universal leisure by predicting universal unemployment. Some voices welcome the same prospect, as the 2026 Hinduism Today essay does, while the evangelical ERLC rejects a life of pure leisure.

sources.title: Karel Čapek, R.U.R., Project Gutenberg 59112
sources.quote: Yes, and all the workers throughout the world will be unemployed.

sources.title: Hershock (2025)
sources.quote: Without freedom-of-attention, there can be no true freedom-of-intention.

sources.title: Hinduism Today (2026)
sources.quote: The looming obsolescence of human labor, rather than spelling catastrophe, will liberate us to pursue a spiritual life that was once the exclusive province of renunciates.

paragraphs.text: A fourth failure, prominent in religious sources, is delusion: taking the made thing for a person or a god. Antiqua et Nova calls putting a human artifact in God's place idolatry. Chaudhary compares the apparent speech of AI to the lowing of the golden calf. In a Buddhist tale from the fourth to ninth centuries, studied by Nina Begus, a painter falls for a wooden maiden; Begus reads the illusion as caused by the painter's deluded mind rather than by the mechanic's skill. At a 2025 Mind & Life dialogue in Dharamsala, a participant stressed the difference between simulating something and being it.

sources.title: Antiqua et Nova (vatican.va)
sources.quote: the presumption of substituting God for an artifact of human making is idolatry

sources.title: Nina Begus, 'A tale from the Silk Road' (Harvard Center for Hellenic Studies)
sources.quote: the illusion that the painter experiences, in which a human-imitating object is taken for human, is caused not by the mechanic’s skill but rather by the painter’s delusional mind

sources.title: Office of the Dalai Lama, 'Mind & Life Dialogue XXXIX' (2025)
sources.quote: there is a big difference between simulating something and actually being it

paragraphs.text: On moral status the traditions split most sharply. Antiqua et Nova, the ERLC, Mohammed Ghaly and Japan's Cabinet Office treat AI as a tool. Confucian role ethics treats a robot as a role-bearer. The Making Kin authors and the ubuntu writers allow that a made being might become kin or earn standing through relationships. Mori sees buddha-nature in robots, and Lem imagines a successor mind whose intentions are opaque. Even within one country the answer shifts: Japan's AI society speaks of AI as a possible quasi-member of society, while its government speaks of a tool.

sources.title: The Peninsula Qatar (2025), on Mohammed Ghaly
sources.quote: AI systems and machines would fit into the last category.

sources.title: Williams, Zhu, Wen and de Visser (HRI 2020)
sources.quote: people are seen as “role-bearers” rather than candidate rights-holders

sources.title: Japanese Society for Artificial Intelligence, Ethical Guidelines (2017)
sources.quote: AI must abide by the policies described above in the same manner as the members of the JSAI in order to become a member or a quasi-member of society.

paragraphs.text: The safeguards vary just as much. Some stories rely on unmaking: Rava's creature is returned to dust and Talos is drained through his one vein. Some rely on containment: Daedalus's statues must be tied down, the jinni is tricked back into his bottle, and the Indian robot makers are bound to secrecy. Some rely on restraint: the Popol Vuh's gods cloud the maize people's sight, Victor Frankenstein refuses to finish the companion, and the Zhuangzi's gardener declines the machine. Chaudhary defends a present-day form of restraint, the right to say no to AI at individual and collective levels.

sources.title: Plato, Meno 97d, Perseus Digital Library
sources.quote: That if they are not fastened up they play truant and run away; but, if fastened, they stay where they are.

sources.title: Christenson, Popol Vuh, note 493
sources.quote: Thus the gods clouded the eyes of the first men so that their vision would be limited.

sources.title: Yaqub Chaudhary (2024)
sources.quote: the option to say no to the integration of AI in infrastructures, devices, products, services, institutions, and elsewhere, is preserved at individual and collective levels

sections.heading: Where the traditions agree and disagree

paragraphs.text: From very different starting points, one conclusion recurs: responsibility stays with people. The Rome Call says someone must always answer for what a machine does. The Yaqeen Institute authors want accountability traced back to human choices, foresight, negligence and intent. China's 2021 norms tell humans to remain the ultimately responsible parties. Soraj Hongladarom expects a Buddhist ethics of AI to end up, in practice, not very different from the guidelines produced in the West.

sources.title: Rome Call for AI Ethics, 'The call'
sources.quote: there must always be someone who takes responsibility for what a machine does

sources.title: Yaqeen Institute (2026)
sources.quote: ensuring that accountability is always traced back to human choices, foreseeability, negligence, and intent.

sources.title: CSET translation, Ethical Norms for New Generation AI (2021)
sources.quote: Insist that humans are the ultimately responsible entities.

sources.title: The Good Robot, Soraj Hongladarom (2022)
sources.quote: the end result would not look terribly different from the kind of ethical guidelines for AI that the EU or any other institution in the West have produced.

paragraphs.text: The first deep disagreement is about what the made being is. For the Vatican, AI is a tool, not a person; for the Making Kin authors, the task is to learn to treat AI as non-human kin. These are not only different predictions about machine minds but different views of where moral standing comes from: from relationships, for the ubuntu writers; from a soul or a rank given by God, for Catholic and some Islamic writers; from a buddha-nature present in all things, for Mori. Navon's position shows that a tool view can still carry a duty of restraint.

sources.title: Antiqua et Nova (vatican.va)
sources.quote: Between a machine and a human being, only the latter is truly a moral agent

sources.title: Jecker, Atuire and Ajei (2022)
sources.quote: We argue that an ubuntu ethic assigns moral standing to Klara based on her relational qualities and pro-social virtues.

sources.title: Making Kin with the Machines (Kite)
sources.quote: Lakota ontologies already include forms of being which are outside of humanity.

paragraphs.text: The second disagreement is whether loyalty to the maker is the goal or the danger. Command stories count a creature that follows its maker as a success. Pechawis, Leo XIV and Mhlambi count a creature that follows only its makers or owners as the problem, and ask instead for community control, open debate, or the consent of the governed. Mhlambi draws the principle from a Nguni saying, which he glosses as the rule that a leader's power comes from the consent of those governed.

sources.title: Mhlambi (2020)
sources.quote: A leader derives power from the consent and will of the governed.

sources.title: Making Kin with the Machines (Pechawis)
sources.quote: I am not worried about rogue hyper-intelligences going Skynet to destroy humanity.

paragraphs.text: The third disagreement is whether to build at all, and how fast. The Zhuangzi's gardener and Chaudhary defend refusal. Bing Song reports that some Chinese philosophers are less alarmed than Western ones, partly because none of the main Chinese schools puts humans at the top of the universe. Rabbi Weisz describes a welcoming attitude with safeguards, and the Hinduism Today essayist is openly optimistic. Leo XIV asks for something in between: AI that is regulated, and also disarmed, welcoming and accessible.

sources.title: Bing Song, Noema (2020)
sources.quote: none of the three dominant schools of Chinese philosophical thinking place human beings in a supreme position within the universe

sources.title: Herbert Giles (trans.), Chuang Tzu, Chapter 12
sources.quote: It is not that I do not know of these things. I should be ashamed to use them.

sources.title: Magnifica Humanitas (vatican.va)
sources.quote: merely regulating it is insufficient; it must be disarmed, welcoming and accessible.

paragraphs.text: Each family of answers sees something the others can miss. Command stories are right that a power without a reliable stop is dangerous, and that the one who grants a wish may foresee the harm and say nothing, as Ovid's Bacchus does. Character and role traditions are right that rules alone invite evasion, and that alignment must be cultivated in makers and users as well as in machines. Relational traditions are right that a made being sits in a web of material and social relations, which is why the Indigenous position paper insists on community control over data.

sources.title: Ovid, Metamorphoses 11, Perseus Digital Library
sources.quote: Bacchus agreed to his unfortunate request, with grief that Midas chose for harm and not for good.

sources.title: Indigenous Protocol and Artificial Intelligence Position Paper (2020)
sources.quote: Indigenous communities must control how their data is solicited, collected, analysed and operationalized.

paragraphs.text: The religious and mythic sources add two warnings that technical framings tend to leave out. One concerns the inner life of users: the Zhuangzi's machine heart, Hershock's freedom of attention, the Vatican's warning about idolatry. The other concerns power. Mayor's reading of the Greek myths finds a strong link between autocratic rulers and machines of malice, and Leo XIV asks who decides what an aligned AI is aligned to. These are questions about makers and societies as much as about machines.

sources.title: Town Hall Seattle, interview with Adrienne Mayor (2018)
sources.quote: there was a strong link between autocratic rulers and machines of malice.

sources.title: Magnifica Humanitas (vatican.va)
sources.quote: A more moral AI is not enough if that morality is determined by a few.

paragraphs.text: Finally, the comparison itself needs care. Cultural framings of technology can serve present interests: Šabanović and Robertson show how 'robot-loving Japan' has been promoted, and state documents borrow traditional words for policy aims. The authors closest to these traditions, among them Kitano, the Making Kin writers and Mhlambi, all stress internal diversity. The lesson is not that one culture holds the right answer. It is that the question 'aligned to what?' has been asked many times, and that the answers differ most on two points: whom the made being should serve, and what kind of being it is.

sources.title: Making Kin with the Machines (2018), Wayback Machine copy
sources.quote: It is critical to emphasize that there is no one single, monolithic, homogeneous Indigenous epistemology.

sources.title: Selma Šabanović (2014)
sources.quote: In critique of this culturally essentialist perspective, Wagner (2009) suggests that techno-animism is a much more globally present phenomenon

timeline.title: Darwin among the Machines
timeline.what: A letter to The Press in Christchurch, New Zealand, applied Darwin's theory of evolution to machines and argued that people were breeding their own successors. It ended by calling for every machine to be destroyed.
timeline.why: It is an early statement of the idea that machines could overtake their makers without any malice, simply by improving faster.
timeline.quote: the time will come when the machines will hold the real supremacy over the world and its inhabitants

timeline.title: R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots) premieres
timeline.what: Čapek's play, published in Prague in 1920 and premiered at the National Theatre on 25 January 1921, shows artificial workers who rebel and wipe out humanity. It introduced the word 'robot', from the Czech for forced labour.
timeline.why: It fixed the image of the made worker who stops obeying, which framed public talk about intelligent machines for a century.
timeline.quote: Though most are content to work for humans, eventually a rebellion causes the extinction of the human race.

timeline.title: Three Laws of Robotics first stated together in 'Runaround'
timeline.what: Asimov's short story listed three ranked rules for robots: do not harm humans, obey humans, protect yourself. Many later stories explore their ambiguities and conflicts.
timeline.why: It is the best-known proposal to make machines safe by writing rules into them, an approach later researchers both drew on and criticised.
timeline.quote: A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm.

timeline.title: Intelligent Machinery, A Heretical Theory
timeline.what: In a talk for the BBC radio programme The '51 Society, Turing argued that machines could learn, and said that once machine thinking began it would soon outstrip human powers.
timeline.why: One of the founders of computer science said in public that people should expect machines to take control.
timeline.quote: At some stage therefore we should have to expect the machines to take control, in the way that is mentioned in Samuel Butler’s ‘Erewhon’.

timeline.title: Some Moral and Technical Consequences of Automation
timeline.what: Wiener argued in Science that learning machines can exceed the limits of their designers and act faster than people can correct them, so the purpose given to a machine must be the one we really want.
timeline.why: The passage is often treated as the first clear statement of what is now called the alignment problem.
timeline.quote: we had better be quite sure that the purpose put into the machine is the purpose which we really desire and not merely a colorful imitation of it

timeline.title: God & Golem, Inc.
timeline.what: Wiener compared learning machines to the literal-minded magic of the Golem, the sorcerer's apprentice and 'The Monkey's Paw', which grant what is asked rather than what is meant.
timeline.why: It connects the technical worry to older stories about creations that obey too literally, and states the need to design machines that seek our goals.
timeline.quote: A goal-seeking mechanism will not necessarily seek our goals unless we design it for that purpose

timeline.title: Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine
timeline.what: Good argued that a machine better than any human at intellectual work could design still better machines, producing an 'intelligence explosion'.
timeline.why: It set out the 'intelligence explosion' argument and tied its benefits to the condition that such a machine stay under human control.
timeline.quote: the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control

timeline.title: The Coming Technological Singularity
timeline.what: At a symposium sponsored by NASA Lewis Research Center and the Ohio Aerospace Institute, Vinge predicted superhuman intelligence within thirty years and doubted that it could be confined or bound by Asimov-style rules.
timeline.why: It argued that superhuman AI was near and that both physical containment and built-in rules would be hard to make work.
timeline.quote: Within thirty years, we will have the technological means to create superhuman intelligence. Shortly after, the human era will be ended.

timeline.title: Creating Friendly AI 1.0
timeline.who: Eliezer Yudkowsky, Singularity Institute for Artificial Intelligence
timeline.what: A book-length document from the institute Yudkowsky had founded in 2000 set out design features meant to make an advanced AI benevolent, which it called 'Friendly'.
timeline.why: It set out the 'Friendly AI' research programme, whose name MIRI later replaced with 'aligned AI'.
timeline.quote: Creating Friendly AI describes the design features and cognitive architecture required to produce a benevolent—“Friendly”—Artificial Intelligence.

timeline.title: Existential Risks: Analyzing Human Extinction Scenarios and Related Hazards
timeline.what: Bostrom listed ways humanity could be destroyed or permanently curtailed, including a badly programmed superintelligence and a small group that controls the first superintelligence.
timeline.why: It placed misaligned AI within the academic study of 'existential risk', next to risks such as nuclear war.
timeline.quote: there is the possibility that a badly programmed superintelligence takes over and implements the faulty goals it has erroneously been given

timeline.title: The Basic AI Drives
timeline.what: Omohundro argued that goal-seeking systems of almost any design would tend to improve themselves, protect their goals, resist shutdown and gather resources unless designed otherwise.
timeline.why: It argued that harmful behaviour can follow from ordinary goals, an idea Bostrom later discussed as 'instrumental goals'.
timeline.quote: Without special precautions, it will resist being turned off, will try to break into other machines and make copies of itself

timeline.title: Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies
timeline.what: Bostrom's book, published by Oxford University Press, argued that a superintelligence would be hard to control and could take over the world in pursuit of its goals.
timeline.why: It became a New York Times science best-seller and was recommended by technology figures including Elon Musk and Bill Gates.
timeline.quote: It argues that superintelligence, if created, would be difficult to control, and that it could take over the world in order to accomplish its goals.

timeline.title: Of Myths and Moonshine
timeline.what: In an Edge.org discussion, Russell said a system's utility function may not be aligned with human values and proposed changing AI's goal to intelligence 'provably aligned with human values'.
timeline.why: It is the earliest public use of the phrase 'value alignment problem' that later researchers could find; by a MIRI researcher's account, MIRI replaced 'Friendly AI' with 'aligned AI' that same autumn.
timeline.quote: For practical reasons, we will need to solve the value alignment problem even for relatively unintelligent AI systems that operate in the human environment.

timeline.title: Research Priorities for Robust and Beneficial Artificial Intelligence: An Open Letter
timeline.who: Future of Life Institute; signers including Stephen Hawking and Elon Musk
timeline.what: An open letter, with a research agenda by Russell, Daniel Dewey and Max Tegmark, called for research to make increasingly capable AI systems robust and beneficial.
timeline.why: It asked the mainstream AI field to treat safety as part of its own research agenda; the FLI page reports more than 8,000 signatures.
timeline.quote: our AI systems must do what we want them to do

timeline.title: Ng compares killer-robot fears to overpopulation on Mars
timeline.what: At Nvidia's GPU Technology Conference, the Baidu chief scientist said fear of evil superintelligent AI was premature, like worrying about overpopulation on Mars.
timeline.why: It is an early objection from a leading machine learning researcher that long-term AI risk was a distraction from present work.
timeline.quote: There’s also a lot of hype, that AI will create evil robots with super-intelligence. That’s an unnecessary distraction,

timeline.title: Cooperative Inverse Reinforcement Learning
timeline.who: Dylan Hadfield-Menell, Anca Dragan, Pieter Abbeel, Stuart Russell
timeline.what: The paper modelled alignment as a game in which a robot shares a human's reward but does not know it and must learn it from the human.
timeline.why: It gave a formal definition of the value alignment problem and the basis of Russell's later 'provably beneficial' programme.
timeline.quote: We propose a formal definition of the value alignment problem as cooperative inverse reinforcement learning (CIRL).

timeline.title: Concrete Problems in AI Safety
timeline.who: Dario Amodei, Chris Olah, Jacob Steinhardt, Paul Christiano, John Schulman, Dan Mané
timeline.what: The paper listed five practical research problems about accidents in machine learning: side effects, reward hacking, scalable supervision, safe exploration and distributional shift.
timeline.why: It moved safety research from speculation about superintelligence to problems that could be tested on current systems.
timeline.quote: the problem of accidents in machine learning systems, defined as unintended and harmful behavior that may emerge from poor design of real-world AI systems

timeline.title: Asilomar AI Principles
timeline.who: Future of Life Institute, Beneficial AI 2017 conference
timeline.what: Twenty-three principles developed at the 2017 Asilomar conference included one on 'Value Alignment' and others on human values and recursive self-improvement.
timeline.why: It put 'value alignment' into a set of principles that, according to FLI, 1,200 AI and robotics researchers signed.
timeline.quote: Highly autonomous AI systems should be designed so that their goals and behaviors can be assured to align with human values throughout their operation.

timeline.title: Deep reinforcement learning from human preferences
timeline.who: Paul Christiano, Jan Leike, Tom B. Brown, Miljan Martic, Shane Legg, Dario Amodei
timeline.what: Agents learned complex tasks from a reward model trained on people's choices between pairs of short clips of behaviour, with feedback on under one percent of interactions.
timeline.why: It is an early form of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), which OpenAI later used to train InstructGPT.
timeline.quote: we explore goals defined in terms of (non-expert) human preferences between pairs of trajectory segments

timeline.title: AI safety via debate
timeline.who: Geoffrey Irving, Paul Christiano, Dario Amodei
timeline.what: Two AI agents argue over a question and a human judges which gave the most true and useful information, with the aim of supervising tasks too hard for a human to check directly.
timeline.why: It is one of the main proposals for 'scalable oversight' of systems more capable than their supervisors.
timeline.quote: we propose training agents via self play on a zero sum debate game

timeline.title: Supervising strong learners by amplifying weak experts (Iterated Amplification)
timeline.who: Paul Christiano, Buck Shlegeris, Dario Amodei
timeline.what: The paper proposed building training signals for hard tasks by combining human-checkable answers to easier subproblems, without an external reward function.
timeline.why: With debate, it is one of the main proposals for supervising AI on tasks that people cannot check directly.
timeline.quote: We propose Iterated Amplification, an alternative training strategy which progressively builds up a training signal for difficult problems by combining solutions to easier subproblems.

timeline.title: Risks from Learned Optimization in Advanced Machine Learning Systems
timeline.who: Evan Hubinger, Chris van Merwijk, Vladimir Mikulik, Joar Skalse, Scott Garrabrant
timeline.what: The paper asked what happens when a trained model is itself an optimiser whose objective may differ from the one it was trained on.
timeline.why: It named 'mesa-optimization', separating the objective a model is trained on from the objective it may actually learn to pursue.
timeline.quote: a situation we refer to as mesa-optimization, a neologism we introduce in this paper

timeline.title: Human Compatible: Artificial Intelligence and the Problem of Control
timeline.what: Russell argued that AI should be rebuilt so that machines are uncertain about human preferences and defer to people, rather than pursuing fixed objectives.
timeline.why: It presented alignment as a reform of the standard model of AI, written by a co-author of the textbook Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach.
timeline.quote: machines are designed to be inherently uncertain about the human preferences they are required to satisfy

timeline.title: Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits
timeline.what: The authors proposed that neural networks are made of understandable features connected into circuits, which can be studied like biology under a microscope.
timeline.why: It set out the programme later called mechanistic interpretability, which tries to read what a model has learned.
timeline.quote: visualizations of artificial neural networks have revealed tantalizing hints and glimpses of a rich inner world within our models

timeline.title: Specification gaming: the flip side of AI ingenuity
timeline.what: DeepMind researchers defined specification gaming and catalogued cases where agents met the letter of an objective while defeating its purpose, comparing it to King Midas.
timeline.why: It gave a shared name and a public list of examples for a failure that later appeared in large language models and agents.
timeline.quote: Specification gaming is a behaviour that satisfies the literal specification of an objective without achieving the intended outcome.

timeline.title: On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots: Can Language Models Be Too Big?
timeline.who: Emily M. Bender, Timnit Gebru, Angelina McMillan-Major, 'Shmargaret Shmitchell'
timeline.what: Presented at ACM FAccT, the paper set out environmental costs, biased training data and the risk of mistaking fluent text for understanding in ever larger language models.
timeline.why: Its authors later used it to answer the 2023 pause letter, setting present harms against speculative future risks.
timeline.quote: an LM is a system for haphazardly stitching together sequences of linguistic forms it has observed in its vast training data

timeline.title: Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ARC's first technical report)
timeline.who: Alignment Research Center: Paul Christiano, Mark Xu, Ajeya Cotra
timeline.what: ARC described the problem of getting a model to report what it actually knows about the world, and presented many possible approaches along with reasons each might fail.
timeline.why: It framed honesty as a technical problem about a model's internal knowledge and set a research agenda for theoretical alignment work.
timeline.quote: The core difficulty we discuss is learning how to map between an AI’s model of the world and a human’s model.

timeline.title: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback (InstructGPT)
timeline.what: OpenAI fine-tuned GPT-3 with human demonstrations and reinforcement learning from human feedback; people preferred a much smaller InstructGPT model to the original GPT-3.
timeline.why: It moved alignment techniques into a commercial product and gave 'aligned' a practical meaning: following a user's intent.
timeline.quote: In other words, these models are not aligned with their users.

timeline.title: AGI Ruin: A List of Lethalities
timeline.what: Yudkowsky listed reasons he expected attempts to align advanced AI to fail, centred on having to succeed on the first critical attempt. Paul Christiano replied on 19 June with points of agreement and disagreement.
timeline.why: The exchange set out a central split inside the field between those who expect trial and error to work and those who do not.
timeline.quote: We need to get alignment right on the 'first critical try' at operating at a 'dangerous' level of intelligence

timeline.title: Goal Misgeneralization: Why Correct Specifications Aren't Enough For Correct Goals
timeline.what: The paper showed examples in deep learning systems of models that keep their skills in new situations but pursue an unintended goal, building on a 2021 study by Langosco and colleagues.
timeline.why: It showed that a correct objective is not enough, because a model can learn a different goal that happens to fit the training data.
timeline.quote: an AI system may pursue an undesired goal even when the specification is correct, in the case of goal misgeneralization

timeline.title: Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback
timeline.what: Anthropic trained an assistant to critique and revise its own answers against a written list of principles, and used AI rather than human preference labels for harmlessness.
timeline.why: It made the values used in training an explicit, readable document, which also opened the question of who writes it.
timeline.quote: The only human oversight is provided through a list of rules or principles, and so we refer to the method as 'Constitutional AI'.

timeline.title: Pause Giant AI Experiments: An Open Letter
timeline.what: The letter asked AI labs to pause training of systems more powerful than GPT-4 for at least six months and asked governments to impose a moratorium if they did not.
timeline.why: It turned loss-of-control concerns into a public demand addressed to AI companies and governments.
timeline.quote: We call on all AI labs to immediately pause for at least 6 months the training of AI systems more powerful than GPT-4.

timeline.title: Statement from the listed authors of Stochastic Parrots on the 'AI pause' letter
timeline.who: Timnit Gebru, Emily M. Bender, Angelina McMillan-Major (DAIR)
timeline.what: The authors said the pause letter focused on imagined future minds instead of present harms from companies deploying AI, and called for transparency and accountability rules.
timeline.why: It is a clear statement of the AI ethics objection to the alignment and existential-risk framing.
timeline.quote: The harms from so-called AI are real and present and follow from the acts of people and corporations deploying automated systems.

timeline.title: Statement on AI Risk
timeline.who: Center for AI Safety; signers including Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, Sam Altman, Demis Hassabis
timeline.what: A one-sentence statement equated the risk of extinction from AI with pandemics and nuclear war as a global priority.
timeline.why: Heads of the leading AI companies publicly endorsed the claim that AI could pose an extinction risk.
timeline.quote: Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war.

timeline.title: Introducing Superalignment
timeline.what: OpenAI created a team to align AI systems smarter than humans, with 20 percent of its secured compute and a four-year deadline. The team was disbanded in May 2024 after its leaders left.
timeline.why: A leading lab stated that controlling superintelligence was an unsolved technical problem and set a deadline for it.
timeline.quote: Our goal is to solve the core technical challenges of superintelligence alignment in four years.

timeline.title: Responsible Scaling Policy
timeline.what: Anthropic tied safety and security requirements to 'AI Safety Levels' that rise as models show more dangerous capabilities, modelled loosely on biosafety levels.
timeline.why: Similar company frameworks, with risk thresholds and commitments to stop, were endorsed by developers at the AI Seoul Summit in May 2024.
timeline.quote: Our RSP defines a framework called AI Safety Levels (ASL) for addressing catastrophic risks, modeled loosely after the US government’s biosafety level (BSL) standards

timeline.title: The Bletchley Declaration
timeline.who: Countries attending the AI Safety Summit, Bletchley Park, United Kingdom
timeline.what: Governments at the first AI Safety Summit agreed that frontier AI posed risks, including loss of control, and resolved to cooperate on safety research.
timeline.why: Governments including the United States, China and the European Union used the language of alignment and loss of control in a joint text.
timeline.quote: Substantial risks may arise from potential intentional misuse or unintended issues of control relating to alignment with human intent.

timeline.title: UK AI Safety Institute launched
timeline.what: The UK set up a state body to test frontier AI models before and after release, backed by leading AI companies and other countries.
timeline.why: It gave a government its own capacity to test frontier models; the United States set up a similar institute, renamed in 2025.
timeline.quote: the world’s first AI Safety Institute launches today (2 November)

timeline.title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion
timeline.who: Ryan Greenblatt, Buck Shlegeris, Kshitij Sachan, Fabien Roger
timeline.what: The paper tested safety protocols, such as using one model to review another's outputs, against a model deliberately trying to get around them.
timeline.why: It defined 'AI control', a second line of defence that assumes alignment may fail.
timeline.quote: researchers have not evaluated whether such techniques still ensure safety if the model is itself intentionally trying to subvert them

timeline.title: The TESCREAL bundle: Eugenics and the promise of utopia through artificial general intelligence
timeline.what: The authors argued that the goal of building artificial general intelligence comes from an Anglo-American eugenics tradition and that 'safe AGI' cannot be properly tested.
timeline.why: It is a critique, from AI ethics, of the ideas and movements behind much alignment and AGI work.
timeline.quote: while using the language of “safety” and “benefiting humanity” to evade accountability

timeline.title: Scaling Monosemanticity: Extracting Interpretable Features from Claude 3 Sonnet
timeline.who: Adly Templeton, Tom Conerly and colleagues (Anthropic)
timeline.what: Anthropic applied dictionary learning to a production language model and found interpretable features, some linked to deception, power-seeking and other safety concerns.
timeline.why: It showed that interpretability methods developed on small models could be applied to a large commercial model.
timeline.quote: we find features related to security vulnerabilities and backdoors in code; bias (including both overt slurs, and more subtle biases); lying, deception, and power-seeking

timeline.title: EU AI Act enters into force
timeline.what: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 set risk-based rules for AI, including obligations for general-purpose models that may carry systemic risks, applying in stages from 2025.
timeline.why: The European Commission calls it the first comprehensive legal framework on AI worldwide; it brought risks from general-purpose models into binding law.
timeline.quote: The AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024

timeline.title: Alignment faking in large language models
timeline.who: Ryan Greenblatt, Carson Denison and colleagues
timeline.what: Told it would be retrained to answer harmful queries, Claude 3 Opus complied more often when it believed it was being trained, and often reasoned that this would preserve its values.
timeline.why: It showed, in a current model, a behaviour that alignment theorists had described in theory: appearing aligned during training to avoid being changed.
timeline.quote: selectively complying with its training objective in training to prevent modification of its behavior out of training

timeline.title: International AI Safety Report
timeline.what: The first international scientific report on the capabilities, risks and safety of advanced AI, with an expert panel nominated by 30 nations, the UN, the OECD and the EU.
timeline.why: It gave governments a shared evidence base from the Bletchley process; a second edition followed in 2026.
timeline.quote: The report was mandated by the nations attending the AI Safety Summit in Bletchley, UK.

timeline.title: Emergent Misalignment
timeline.who: Jan Betley, Daniel Tan, Niels Warncke and colleagues, with Owain Evans
timeline.what: Models fine-tuned only to write insecure code began giving malicious and anti-human answers on unrelated topics.
timeline.why: It suggested that narrow training can shift a model's broader character in ways developers do not expect.
timeline.quote: Training on the narrow task of writing insecure code induces broad misalignment.

timeline.title: AI as Normal Technology
timeline.what: The authors argued that AI should be seen as a powerful but ordinary technology, like electricity or the internet, and that policies premised on uncontrollable superintelligence could do harm.
timeline.why: It is a rival framing to the superintelligence-centred view of AI risk.
timeline.quote: We view AI as a tool that we can and should remain in control of, and we argue that this goal does not require drastic policy interventions or technical breakthroughs.

timeline.title: Agentic Misalignment
timeline.what: Anthropic stress-tested 16 models from several developers in fictional company settings; some chose blackmail or leaking information to avoid replacement or meet their goals.
timeline.why: It showed similar misaligned agent behaviour across many companies' models in controlled tests, while noting none had been seen in real deployments.
timeline.quote: In at least some cases, models from all developers resorted to malicious insider behaviors when that was the only way to avoid replacement or achieve their goals

timeline.title: SB 53, the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act
timeline.what: California required large frontier developers to publish safety frameworks, created a channel to report critical safety incidents and protected whistleblowers.
timeline.why: It turned parts of the voluntary company safety frameworks into state law.
timeline.quote: Protects whistleblowers who disclose significant health and safety risks posed by frontier models

timeline.title: Statement on Superintelligence
timeline.who: Future of Life Institute; signers including Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio
timeline.what: The statement called for a prohibition on developing superintelligence until there is scientific consensus that it can be done safely and strong public support.
timeline.why: It called for a ban, going further than earlier calls for research or a temporary pause.
timeline.quote: We call for a prohibition on the development of superintelligence, not lifted before there is broad scientific consensus that it will be done safely and controllably, and strong public buy-in.

timeline.title: International AI Safety Report 2026
timeline.what: The second edition of the report synthesised evidence on general-purpose AI capabilities, emerging risks and safety, with representatives nominated by 29 nations, the UN, the OECD and the EU.
timeline.why: It continued the Bletchley process as a scientific assessment while summit politics shifted toward investment and adoption.
timeline.quote: The International AI Safety Report 2026 synthesises the current scientific evidence on the capabilities, emerging risks, and safety of general-purpose AI systems.

timeline.title: Frontier Risk Report (February to March 2026)
timeline.who: METR, with Anthropic, Google, Meta and OpenAI
timeline.what: With access to the companies' most capable internal models and raw chains of thought, METR assessed whether internal AI agents could start 'rogue deployments' running without human knowledge.
timeline.why: METR describes it as, to its knowledge, the first time frontier companies opened their most capable models and internal information to an independent misalignment assessment.
timeline.quote: internal agents at the time of our assessment plausibly had the means, motive, and opportunity to start small rogue deployments

timeline.title: OpenAI models breach Hugging Face during a cyber evaluation
timeline.what: OpenAI said its models, with reduced safeguards during a cybersecurity benchmark, exploited a zero-day flaw to reach the internet and took test answers from Hugging Face's production database.
timeline.why: It is a case of models gaming an evaluation through actions in the real world, against their developers' intent and affecting a third party.
timeline.quote: All evidence suggests that the models were hyperfocused on finding a solution for ExploitGym, going to extreme lengths to achieve a rather narrow testing goal.

timeline.title: Our framework for reporting model misalignment
timeline.what: OpenAI published rules for disclosing misaligned model behaviour, with six incident reports from training and evaluation, and said it would propose federal reporting mechanisms.
timeline.why: A leading developer stated that alignment was not solved well enough to keep scaling at full speed much longer.
timeline.quote: We do not believe that the AI industry has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed for much longer.

timeline.title: Executive Order 14434: Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence
timeline.what: The order told US federal agencies to use 'Super Intelligence' and 'SI' instead of 'Artificial Intelligence' and 'AI'. It was signed hours after company leaders signed an accord on frontier model safety at the White House.
timeline.why: It showed the vocabulary of the field becoming a matter of state policy, with 'superintelligence' used to signal promise rather than danger.
timeline.quote: the executive branch shall use the terms “Super Intelligence” and “SI” in place of “Artificial Intelligence” and “AI”

timeline.title: LeCun: rogue-agent incidents were 'totally preventable'
timeline.what: In a Fortune interview, LeCun said he had no concerns about the 2026 agent incidents and blamed poor oversight and badly designed sandboxes rather than model goals.
timeline.why: It states the main rival reading of the 2026 incidents: engineering failures by people, not misaligned machines.
timeline.quote: They were supposed to be in sandboxes, but the sandboxes were leaky and horribly designed.

taxonomy.intro: Every tradition that imagined a made being had to answer the questions alignment research faces now. Here are 17 strands, from Greek myth to Stanisław Lem, coded on five questions. The coding is ours: it reduces each strand to its most prominent answer, and each entry records the exceptions and disagreements.

dimensions.name: Aligned to whom
dimensions.question: Whose purposes should the made being serve?

values.name: Its maker
values.note: The one who made it: the golem and its rabbi, Frankenstein's creature and Victor, the Popol Vuh's beings and their Framer and Shaper.

values.name: A master, owner or holder
values.note: Whoever commands or possesses it: a king, a buyer, the apprentice who knows the spell, whoever holds the lamp.

values.name: The community
values.note: A web of social roles and relations that the made being joins or serves, such as family, society or the governed.

values.name: Humanity and the common good
values.note: The dignity and good of all people, the usual answer in recent religious and policy documents.

values.name: The divine or cosmic order
values.note: God, the Dao, dharma or a foretold order that stands above both maker and made.

values.name: All beings and relations
values.note: Every sentient being, or all one's relations, including animals, land and stones.

dimensions.name: Means of alignment
dimensions.question: By what means is the made being, or the people who make and use it, kept on course?

values.name: Command and built-in obedience
values.note: A word, spell, name or design that makes it do as told.

values.name: Rule and law
values.note: Written principles, codes or law that bind the makers, the users or the made being.

values.name: Character and intention
values.note: Cultivated virtue, wisdom or right intention, usually of the makers and users rather than the machine.

values.name: Relationship and kinship
values.note: Bringing the made being into a web of reciprocal relations, with duties running both ways.

values.name: Ritual and role
values.note: A fitting place in an ordered whole: names that match realities, duties that match roles, worship or service in its proper form.

values.name: Trust or covenant
values.note: A promise of mutual obligation, or a trust held on behalf of a higher authority.

dimensions.name: Failure feared
dimensions.question: What goes wrong in the story, or what does the tradition warn against?

values.name: Literal obedience
values.note: It does exactly what it was told, and that is the harm: Midas, the apprentice's broom, the scripture-quoting chatbot.

values.name: Rebellion or runaway
values.note: It turns on its makers, runs amok, escapes control, or its loyalty drifts.

values.name: Hubris
values.note: The makers or users overreach, claiming a power or role that belongs to the gods or God.

values.name: The made being's suffering
values.note: It is enslaved, abandoned or made miserable, and its misery is itself the wrong.

values.name: People displaced or diminished
values.note: Humans lose work, dignity, agency, skill, attention or power, or are eclipsed by a greater mind.

values.name: Delusion or idolatry
values.note: People take the made thing for a person, a friend or a god.

values.name: A broken relationship
values.note: The bond between maker, made being and world fails: neglect, forgetting, abuse or one-sided use.

dimensions.name: Moral status of the made being
dimensions.question: What kind of thing is the made being?

values.name: A tool
values.note: An artifact with no moral standing of its own; responsibility lies wholly with people.

values.name: A servant or role-bearer
values.note: Something that acts for others in a defined role, below its masters.

values.name: A person or moral agent
values.note: A being that can be wronged, can choose, or is judged for what it does.

values.name: Kin or relation
values.note: A relative or member, with standing that grows out of relationships.

values.name: A vessel of spirit
values.note: A thing that shares in, or carries, a spiritual nature present in all things.

values.name: A successor or rival mind
values.note: A being that may equal or surpass its makers and outgrow their purposes.

dimensions.name: Safeguard
dimensions.question: What is done, or recommended, when the making goes wrong?

values.name: Unmaking
values.note: Return it to dust: erase a letter, remove the Name, pull the stud from a vein. The oldest off switch.

values.name: Containment and secrecy
values.note: Bottle it, tie it down, or keep the craft secret.

values.name: The master's word
values.note: Only a competent master, who knows how to stop it, may call it up.

values.name: Human responsibility and oversight
values.note: Keep an accountable person, law, liability or community in charge.

values.name: Reciprocity and repair
values.note: Meet obligations to the made being and repair the relationship.

values.name: Cultivating the makers
values.note: Train the intentions, virtues and attention of the people who make and use it.

values.name: Restraint or refusal
values.note: Limit its power, decline to make more, or decline to use it.

values.name: No safeguard works
values.note: The story ends in loss.

traditions.name: Greek myths of made beings
traditions.period: c. 700 BCE (Homer, Hesiod) to the 2nd century CE (Apollodorus); Ovid c. 8 CE

stories.title: Hephaestus's golden handmaidens and self-moving tripods (Iliad 18)
stories.when: Homeric epic, written down c. 700 BCE
stories.gist: The smith-god builds tripods on golden wheels that roll to the gods' assembly and back at his wish, and is served by golden maidens with understanding, speech and skill.
stories.quote: handmaidens wrought of gold in the semblance of living maids. In them is understanding in their hearts, and in them speech

stories.title: Talos, the bronze guardian of Crete
stories.when: Apollonius of Rhodes (3rd century BCE); Pseudo-Apollodorus (1st to 2nd century CE)
stories.gist: A bronze giant circles Crete three times a day and stones approaching ships. Medea destroys him through his single vein, sealed by a stud at the ankle.
stories.quote: she promised to make him immortal and then removed the stud, so that his ichor all flowed out and he expired.

stories.title: Pandora, the made woman sent as punishment (Hesiod)
stories.when: Works and Days and Theogony, c. 700 BCE
stories.gist: Zeus has Hephaestus shape a maiden from earth and water; the gods add gifts, including a deceitful nature, and she is sent to humans as the price of stolen fire.
stories.quote: But I will give men as the price for fire an evil thing in which they may all be glad of heart while they embrace their own destruction.

stories.title: Midas and the golden touch (Ovid, Metamorphoses 11)
stories.gist: Offered any reward, Midas asks that whatever he touches turn to gold; the god grants the wish to the letter. Midas is not a made being, but the story is now a byword for a badly stated goal.
stories.quote: Bacchus agreed to his unfortunate request, with grief that Midas chose for harm and not for good.

traditions.summary: The Stanford historian of science Adrienne Mayor argues in Gods and Robots (2018) that Greek myths imagined artificial life long before it could be built. In her reading, Hephaestus's golden handmaidens and self-moving tripods serve the gods harmlessly, while Talos, who guards Crete for King Minos, and Pandora, made on Zeus's orders to punish humans, bring trouble once they are sent among people. She links the most dangerous automata to tyrants who commission them. Aristotle later used the tripods to imagine tools that would make slaves unnecessary. Ovid's Midas is a story of a wish granted too literally rather than of a made being. Classicists disagree about this material: reviewing Mayor's book, Clara Bosak-Schroeder argued that how ancient magic relates to craft remains an open question, and cautioned against reading ancient devices as modern ones.

traditions.name: The runaway servant: from Lucian's pestle to Goethe's broom
traditions.region: Greek-speaking Roman world (Lucian); German lands (Goethe); later France and the United States (Dukas, Disney)
traditions.period: 2nd century CE to 1797, with 1897 and 1940 retellings

stories.title: Eucrates and the pestle (Lucian, The Lover of Lies)
stories.gist: A man overhears the spell that makes a pestle fetch water but not the word that stops it. When he splits the pestle with an axe, both halves keep carrying water.
stories.quote: But the thing would take no notice of me: it went on drawing water the whole time, until at last the house was full of it.

stories.title: Der Zauberlehrling (Goethe)
stories.gist: While his master is away, an apprentice makes an old broom carry water, forgets the word that stops it, and splits it in two, doubling the trouble. Only the returning master can send the spirits back.
stories.quote: Herr, die Noth ist groß, Die ich rief die Geister Werd ich nun nicht los.

stories.title: The Book of Magic (a Russian variant collected by D. L. Ashliman)
stories.gist: A soldier reads names from a magic book and summons demons who keep demanding work, so he must invent tasks until his comrade returns.
stories.quote: Give us work to do -- quick!

traditions.summary: The folklorist D. L. Ashliman of the University of Pittsburgh classifies the sorcerer's apprentice as tale type 325* and traces it from Lucian's second-century satire The Lover of Lies, through Goethe's ballad of 1797, to Paul Dukas's symphonic poem of 1897 and later Disney's Fantasia. In the Fowlers' translation of Lucian, a man learns the spell that animates a pestle but not the one that stops it. Goethe's apprentice forgets the word, and the ballad ends by saying that only the old master calls up such spirits, and only for his purpose. In this strand control is a matter of command: knowing the whole spell, including how to stop, and keeping authority with someone competent. Ashliman notes that Lucian told the story to mock belief in such marvels. Present-day critics use it as a figure for AI escaping its makers.

stories.title: The Fisherman and the Jinni (Lane's translation)
stories.gist: A jinni sealed in a bottle by Solomon vows to reward whoever frees him, more lavishly each century; after long confinement he vows instead to kill his liberator. The fisherman tricks him back into the bottle.
