stories.title: Aladdin and the slave of the lamp
stories.when: Added by Antoine Galland from the Aleppine storyteller Hanna Diyab, early 18th century
stories.gist: The genie serves whoever holds the lamp, so a rival who steals it can command it. Yet it refuses one order, to bring its own master, and names who is really behind the request.
stories.quote: I am ready to obey thee as thy slave, and the slave of all those who have that lamp in their hands; I, and the other slaves of the lamp.

traditions.summary: In Edward William Lane's translation of the Nights, a jinni sealed in a bottle by Solomon first vows to reward whoever frees him, then, after centuries of confinement, vows to kill that person; the fisherman who frees him survives by reason, not force. Aladdin's genie, which research by Paulo Lemos Horta traces to the Aleppine storyteller Hanna Diyab, serves whoever holds the lamp, yet refuses an order against its own master and names the real author of the request. The literary scholar Marina Warner describes jinn as intermediate, unpredictable beings, redeemable in Islamic teaching, and bound to whoever chance makes their master. Jinn are not made by humans, so this strand concerns bound rather than built servants. In it the servant is also a moral agent whose loyalty can drift.

traditions.name: The golem in Jewish tradition
traditions.region: Babylonia; medieval Rhineland (Kabbalah); Bohemia and Poland; Israel and the diaspora
traditions.period: Babylonian Talmud (Rava, 4th century CE) to the present

stories.title: Rava's man (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 65b)
stories.when: Talmudic; Rava lived in the 4th century CE
stories.gist: The sage Rava makes a man and sends him to Rabbi Zeira, who speaks to him and gets no answer, concludes he was made by a sage, and tells him to return to dust.
stories.quote: Rabbi Zeira would speak to him but he would not reply.

stories.title: Jeremiah's golem and the word for truth
stories.when: Medieval Kabbalistic tale, retold by Gershom Scholem in 1965
stories.gist: Jeremiah and his son make a man with 'truth' (emet) on his forehead. The creature erases one letter, leaving 'dead' (met), to warn its makers that their act edges toward blasphemy.
stories.quote: But this newly created man had a knife in his hand, with which he erased the letter aleph from the word emeth (“truth”); there remained the word meth (“dead”).

stories.title: The Golem of Prague (Rabbi Judah Loew, the Maharal)
stories.when: Legend first recorded in the 19th century; popularized by Yudl Rosenberg's 1909 book
stories.gist: Rabbi Loew's clay golem works for, and in later versions protects, Prague's Jews. He deactivates it each Sabbath by removing the Name; one week he forgets and it runs amok.
stories.quote: Every Sabbath the Rabbi would remove the slip of paper with the Name of God on it, and the Golem would become inanimate for the day

traditions.summary: In the Babylonian Talmud (Sanhedrin 65b) the sage Rava makes a man who cannot answer speech, and Rabbi Zeira sends it back to dust. Gershom Scholem (1965) describes medieval Kabbalists who tied golem-making to letter combinations and to the word emet, truth, and defines the golem as a servant that may outgrow its maker's control. The best-known version, Rabbi Loew's clay servant in Prague, is modern: Curt Leviant, writing for the National Endowment for the Humanities, shows that it first appears in the nineteenth century and spread through Yudl Rosenberg's 1909 book. Scholem and Norbert Wiener both linked the golem to the computer. Present-day rabbis differ: Rabbi Eliezer Simha Weisz describes a welcoming attitude to AI with safeguards, while Rabbi Mois Navon denies that current AI has experience and warns against making a being that could be owned as a person.

traditions.summary: Catholic documents place AI within a theology of the human person, made in God's image and called to care for creation. The Vatican's Antiqua et Nova (2025) calls AI 'a tool, not a person', says only humans are moral agents, and warns against idolatry and against benefits for the few at the cost of many. The Rome Call (2020) sets out principles for makers and insists that someone always answer for what a machine does. Pope Leo XIV chose his name with AI in mind, and his encyclical Magnifica Humanitas (2026) argues that aligning AI with human values is not enough if a few decide what those values are. The evangelical ERLC statement (2019) also denies machines moral agency and rejects a life of pure leisure. Russian Orthodox views, according to one Orthodox commentator, range from apocalyptic warnings to pragmatic acceptance, with no official document yet.

traditions.summary: Muslim scholars writing on AI often begin from Qur'anic concepts rather than from a myth of a made being. Qur'an 33:72 describes a Trust (amanah) that the heavens, earth and mountains declined and humans accepted; 2:30 calls the human a khalifa, a deputy or successor, a choice the angels questioned. Translators render both words differently. In 34:12-14 jinn labour for Solomon under command and do not notice his death. Al-Jazari's automata (c. 1206) served at court. Present-day voices differ. Mohammed Ghaly of Hamad Bin Khalifa University ranks AI among inanimate things and excludes it from worship. Authors at the Yaqeen Institute (2026) call developers' work stewardship and keep liability with humans. Yaqub Chaudhary warns against venerating AI and defends the right to refuse it. Sheikh Abdallah bin Bayyah calls for shared religious values so that AI does not become 'intelligence without conscience'.

traditions.name: Daoist texts: the artificer and the machine heart
traditions.period: Daodejing c. 4th century BCE; Zhuangzi (layered, Warring States to early Han); Liezi compiled c. 4th century CE; present-day commentary

stories.title: Yan Shi's automaton (Liezi, 'Tang Wen' chapter)
stories.when: Compiled c. 4th century CE; set in the reign of King Mu of Zhou
stories.gist: The artificer Yan Shi presents King Mu with a singing figure. When it flirts with the king's ladies, the king nearly executes its maker, until Yan Shi takes it apart to show it is leather, wood, glue and paint.
stories.quote: the automaton winked his eye and made sundry advances to the ladies in attendance on the King

stories.title: The gardener who refuses the well-sweep (Zhuangzi, 'Heaven and Earth')
stories.gist: Confucius's disciple Zigong urges an old gardener to use a labour-saving well-sweep. The gardener refuses: cunning implements, his teacher said, make cunning dealings and cunning hearts.
stories.quote: those who have cunning implements are cunning in their dealings, and that those who are cunning in their dealings have cunning in their hearts

stories.title: More implements, more disorder (Daodejing 57)

stories.quote: the more implements to add to their profit that the people have, the greater disorder is there in the state and clan

traditions.summary: Two texts conventionally classed as Daoist treat made things in different ways. In the Liezi, compiled around the fourth century CE, the artificer Yan Shi presents King Mu with a lifelike automaton; when it flirts with the court ladies the king nearly executes its maker, until the figure is shown to be leather, wood, glue and paint (Lionel Giles's 1912 translation). The king then asks whether human skill can rival 'the maker of transformations'. In the Zhuangzi, a gardener refuses a labour-saving device because, his teacher said, cunning implements breed cunning hearts (Herbert Giles, 1889). The Daodejing links more implements and more laws to more disorder. Today the philosopher Yuk Hui and the Berggruen Institute's Bing Song draw on Daoist ideas to question Western framings of AI; both are their own generalisations about Chinese thought.

traditions.name: Confucian role ethics: names, ritual and harmony
traditions.region: China and the wider East Asian Confucian world
traditions.period: Analects c. 5th to 3rd century BCE; present-day scholarship and documents 2019-2025

stories.title: Rectification of names (Analects 13.3)
stories.when: Analects, compiled c. 5th to 3rd century BCE
stories.gist: Asked what he would do first in government, Confucius says he would rectify names: when names do not match realities, speech, affairs, ritual and punishment all go astray.
stories.quote: If names be not correct, language is not in accordance with the truth of things.

stories.title: Led by virtue, not by law (Analects 2.3)
stories.gist: People governed by laws and punishments learn to avoid punishment without shame; people led by virtue and ritual develop shame and become good.
stories.quote: If the people be led by laws, and uniformity sought to be given them by punishments, they will try to avoid the punishment, but have no sense of shame.

stories.title: Let the prince be prince (Analects 12.11)
stories.gist: Order exists when each person fulfils the role they hold: ruler, minister, father, son.
stories.quote: There is government, when the prince is prince, and the minister is minister; when the father is father, and the son is son.

traditions.summary: The Analects attributes to Confucius two linked ideas: government begins by rectifying names, so that each person lives up to the role they hold, and people led by virtue and ritual become good, while people led by law only learn to avoid punishment (James Legge's translation). Some modern scholars read this as a role ethics in which persons are role-bearers rather than rights-holders; others read it as virtue or care ethics. Tom Williams, Qin Zhu and colleagues (2020) offer role ethics as a frame for robots that should sometimes remonstrate. Pak-Hang Wong (2025) uses Confucian accounts of trust to widen the idea of trustworthy AI. Yi Zeng, lead drafter of the Beijing AI Principles (2019), traces their ideal of harmony to Confucian thought. State documents borrow this language but are not the tradition's voice. Bing Song reports that Confucian scholars worry most about robots in family care.

today.quote: people are seen as “role-bearers” rather than candidate rights-holders

traditions.summary: Several distinct strands are often merged under the word 'Japan'. Edo-period karakuri dolls, such as the tea-serving doll in Hosokawa Hanzō's Karakuri zui (1796), performed small services at a master's cue. In 1928 the biologist Makoto Nishimura built Gakutensoku as a reply to Čapek's enslaved robots: a friend he called one of 'Nature's grandchildren' (Yulia Frumer, 2020). The roboticist Masahiro Mori argued that robots share buddha-nature and that control is reciprocal. Naho Kitano (2007) links robot acceptance to animism and to rinri, ethics as harmony in relationships. Jennifer Robertson and Selma Šabanović show that the image of robot-loving Japan was partly produced by state and industry, and surveys do not support Japanese exceptionalism. Present-day documents differ as well: the Japanese Society for AI's guidelines (2017) ask AI itself to follow ethics as a possible member of society, while the Cabinet Office (2019) treats AI as a tool.

traditions.name: Hindu and wider Indian yantra traditions
traditions.region: South Asia, with present-day voices in India and the diaspora
traditions.period: Legends set in the 5th to 3rd centuries BCE but written down later; the Samarangana Sutradhara (11th century CE); present day

stories.title: The robot guardians of the Buddha's relics (Lokapannatti)
stories.when: Set under Ajatasatru and Asoka; the written version is later and its date is disputed
stories.gist: As retold by Adrienne Mayor, King Ajatasatru's 'spirit movement machines' guard the Buddha's relics until a foretold king arrives; Asoka fights them and ends up commanding them. Their makers are bound to secrecy by force.
stories.quote: According to the story, it was foretold that Ajatasatru’s robots would remain on duty until a future king would distribute Buddha’s relics throughout the realm.

stories.when: 11th century CE; attributed to King Bhoja of Dhar, authorship uncertain

stories.quote: not explain how to construct such machines, for the sake of secrecy, and not due to lack of knowledge.

stories.title: One's own task (Bhagavad Gita 3.35)
stories.when: Classical text; Edwin Arnold's verse translation
stories.gist: Krishna teaches that it is better to do one's own appointed task imperfectly than another's well, an ethic of duty in role.
stories.quote: this is better, that one do His own task as he may, even though he fail, Than take tasks not his own, though they seem good.

traditions.summary: Adrienne Mayor retells a legend from the Lokapannatti, a Pali Buddhist text, in which automaton guards called 'bhuta vahana yanta' protect the Buddha's relics for King Ajatasatru until a foretold king, Asoka, defeats and then commands them, while the robot makers' secrets are guarded by robotic assassins. Mayor notes that most scholars date the story to medieval times; she argues it may be older. The Samarangana Sutradhara, attributed to King Bhoja (11th century), describes mechanical dolls for palaces and withholds construction details for secrecy. Signe Cohen's I, Yantra (2024) translates Hindu, Buddhist and Jain robot tales and reads them as reflections on personhood. Present-day voices disagree: Chinmay Pandya warns that AI may rob people of purpose, a Hinduism Today essayist welcomes the end of labour, and Swami Sarvapriyananda and Subhash Kak each separate machine intelligence from consciousness.

traditions.name: Buddhist ethics of intention
traditions.region: South, Southeast, Central and East Asia, and global communities
traditions.period: Early Buddhist texts; a mechanical-maiden tale in versions from about the 4th to 9th centuries CE; present day

stories.title: Intention is kamma (Anguttara Nikaya 6.63)
stories.gist: The Buddha defines kamma, moral action, as intention acted out through body, speech and mind, placing intention at the centre of ethics.
stories.quote: Intention, I tell you, is kamma. Intending, one does kamma by way of body, speech, & intellect.

stories.title: The puppet with no maker (Samyutta Nikaya 5.9)
stories.gist: Mara asks the nun Sela who made 'this puppet', the human person; she answers that it arises from causes, turning the question of a maker into one of dependent arising.
stories.quote: This puppet isn’t self-made, nor is this gloom made by another. It comes to be because of a cause, and ceases when the cause breaks up.

stories.title: The Painter and the Mechanical Maiden
stories.when: Buddhist texts from roughly the 4th to 9th centuries CE
stories.gist: A mechanic places a wooden maiden in his guest's bed; the painter falls for her until she comes apart. Nina Begus reads the tale as a lesson about illusion.
stories.quote: In order to serve his guest at his best, the mechanic puts a wooden mechanical maiden on the painter’s bed.

traditions.summary: Buddhist sources place ethics in intention: the Anguttara Nikaya defines kamma as intention, and the Metta Sutta asks practitioners to cherish all living beings. An early text answers the question 'who made this puppet?' with causes rather than a maker. Nina Begus traces a Buddhist tale in which a mechanical maiden deceives a painter, and reads its warning as one about the viewer's delusion. Present-day voices differ on the machine itself. Masahiro Mori (1974) held that robots share buddha-nature. Soraj Hongladarom proposes 'machine enlightenment' as a design ideal but calls it a metaphor. Peter Hershock argues that technical alignment is not enough, because AI amplifies human craving and erodes attention. The Dalai Lama's office reports his view that AI, made by human intelligence, will not take over. Stefania Travagnin asks whether AI is a skilful means or a spiritual friend.

traditions.region: Southern Africa (Nguni and Sotho-Tswana communities); used more widely in African philosophy and African Union policy
traditions.period: Oral tradition; written by African philosophers in the 20th century; applied to AI from 2020

stories.title: Umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu: a person is a person through other persons
stories.when: Nguni oral tradition, cited in Mhlambi 2020
stories.gist: A Nguni saying ties a person's personhood to their relations with others; Mhlambi takes it as the basis for an AI ethic that does not rest personhood on rationality.
stories.quote: It is often expressed in the phrase umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu which emphasises ‘communality and the inter-dependence of the members of a community’

stories.title: 'Wo, akumuntu lowo' (Oh, that is no person)
stories.when: Everyday Nguni usage, described by Mhlambi 2020
stories.gist: Personhood is something achieved through how one treats others, and can be failed; Mhlambi treats it as a matter of degree earned through conduct.
stories.quote: When a person fails at achieving ubuntu, It is common in Nguni languages to say “Wo, akumuntu lowo” (Oh, that is no person)

stories.title: Klara and Adam read through ubuntu
stories.gist: Jecker, Atuire and Ajei apply ubuntu to robots from two novels: Ishiguro's caring Klara gains moral standing through relationships, while McEwan's rational but unattached Adam does not.
stories.quote: We argue that an ubuntu ethic assigns moral standing to Klara based on her relational qualities and pro-social virtues.

traditions.summary: Sabelo Mhlambi, writing for the Carr Center at Harvard Kennedy School in 2020, sets ubuntu, which he presents as Nguni philosophy, against the Western habit of grounding personhood in rationality. He argues that this habit shaped AI and lies behind harms such as discrimination, surveillance and data colonialism. In his reading a person becomes a person through relations with the community, the environment and the spiritual realm; power is legitimate only with the consent of the governed, so technology should come under community control. Nancy Jecker, Caesar Atuire and Martin Odei Ajei (2022) apply the frame to robots, holding that moral standing can be earned through relationships. The African Union's 2024 AI strategy names ubuntu among African values. Mhlambi himself quotes the view that ubuntu is distinctly southern African, so treating it as a pan-African doctrine generalises.

today.who: Sabelo Mhlambi, Technology and Human Rights Fellow, Carr Center for Human Rights Policy, Harvard Kennedy School
today.what: Argues that ubuntu's relational personhood answers the ethical limits of treating rationality as personhood, and proposes community-centred AI governance.
today.quote: The relational Sub-Saharan African philosophy of ubuntu reconciles the ethical limitations of rationality as personhood by linking one’s personhood to the personhood of others.

today.who: Nancy S. Jecker, Caesar A. Atuire and Martin Odei Ajei (with the University of Ghana)

today.quote: We argue that Adam is not a person in the African sense; however, he qualifies as a person according to many standard Western views, such as Kantian and utilitarian ethics.

today.quote: values such as Ubuntu, which respects collective community over individuality

traditions.name: Indigenous relational protocols (Kanaka Maoli, Cree, Lakota and others)
traditions.region: North America and the Pacific, as represented in the 2018 essay and the 2019 Honolulu workshops

stories.title: Hāloa, the long breath (Kanaka Maoli)
stories.when: Hawaiian moʻolelo, read for AI by Noelani Arista in 2018
stories.gist: The stillborn child Hāloa is buried and the first kalo (taro) grows from his body; Arista uses this genealogy of mutual care to ask how relations between humans and AI can be made balanced.
stories.quote: Rather than holding AI separate or beneath, might we consider how we cultivate reciprocal relationships

stories.title: Kinship terms for an AI (nēhiyaw, Plains Cree)
stories.gist: Asked whether AIs could join the circle of kinship, the Cree knowledge keeper Keith Goulet turned at once to how one would address them, and said yes, with a proviso.
stories.quote: If it happens to be an Artificial Intelligence which is a younger person, it would be nisîmis (my younger brother or sister)

stories.title: Stones as ancestors (Lakota)
stories.gist: Suzanne Kite recalls her grandfather speaking of stones as ancestors; since AI is built from minerals, relations with AI are also relations with mines and stones.
stories.quote: Forming a relationship to AI, we form a relationship to the mines and the stones.

traditions.summary: Two collective texts set out this strand: 'Making Kin with the Machines' (Jason Edward Lewis, Noelani Arista, Archer Pechawis and Suzanne Kite, 2018) and the Indigenous Protocol and Artificial Intelligence Position Paper (2020), which grew from workshops in Honolulu. Both draw on the knowledge of specific peoples, among them Kanaka Maoli, Plains Cree and Lakota, and both say they do not speak for all Indigenous peoples. They propose bringing AI into a circle of relations governed by each community's protocols, instead of treating it as a tool or a slave, and they tie AI's ethics to its whole material stack, down to the mines. Pechawis fears not a rogue AI but powerful systems that repeat their makers' mistakes. The authors record open disagreement: most of Pechawis's Native dinner guests opposed kinship with AI.

stories.when: Popol Vuh, creation of the first four people

traditions.summary: In Allen J. Christenson's translation of the Popol Vuh, the creator gods make beings so that someone will remember, worship and sustain them with intelligible speech. Christenson's notes say each failed creation is undone mainly because it cannot speak and understand in this way. The mud being dissolves; the wooden effigies multiply but have no heart or mind and do not remember their makers, and their own mistreated animals and kitchen tools turn on them. The successful maize people see too much, so the gods limit their sight. One text thus holds several failures: a made being without understanding, tools that revolt against abuse, and makers who curb a creation's power. The text was written down under colonial rule and survives in a colonial copy. No present-day K'iche' voice on AI was found; the 'today' entries are regional Latin American voices, not voices of this tradition.

traditions.summary: In the 1818 text of Mary Shelley's novel, the alignment problem runs both ways. Victor Frankenstein dreams that a new species would bless him as its creator, then abandons the being he made. The creature reasons that he was benevolent until misery made him a fiend, and offers to be docile to his 'natural lord and king' if Victor performs his part: a covenant of mutual obligation, which Victor breaks. Victor's later fear, that a breeding pair might found 'a race of devils', is a fear of a self-reproducing creation beyond control, and he answers it by refusing to finish the companion. In 2017 editors at Arizona State University published the novel for scientists and engineers as a study of creativity and responsibility, and Carnegie Mellon University used the bicentennial to discuss AI.

traditions.name: Karel Čapek's R.U.R. and the invention of the robot

stories.title: Rossum's cheapest worker
stories.gist: The factory director explains that young Rossum simplified the human being into a worker with minimal needs, stripped of everything that does not serve work.
stories.quote: Young Rossum invented a worker with the minimum amount of requirements. He had to simplify him.

stories.title: Helena asks for souls
stories.gist: Helena persuaded Dr Gall to make the Robots more like humans, hoping they would then understand people; later she burns Rossum's formula.
stories.quote: I asked him to give the Robots souls.

stories.title: The Robots' revolt
stories.gist: The Robots kill humanity but spare Alquist, the builder, and their leader proclaims the rule of the Robots.
stories.quote: the power of man has fallen. A new world has arisen, the rule of the Robots, march.

traditions.summary: In R.U.R., Čapek imagines artificial workers made by chemistry and sold as the cheapest labour, deliberately stripped of everything that does not serve work. The play stages nearly every failure in this taxonomy. The owners promise an end to toil, but a sceptic predicts mass unemployment; the Robots are treated as things; Helena's humane intervention gives them feeling, which contributes to their revolt; humanity is destroyed; and the play ends with two Robots who love each other inheriting the earth. The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction notes that 'robot' comes from the Czech robota, statute labour, and reads the play as a comment on slavery. Čapek credited the word to his brother Josef, and in 1935 he protested that his robots were not machines of metal and cogwheels. The English text on Project Gutenberg is the 1923 Selver and Playfair adaptation.

traditions.summary: Lem's Golem XIV imagines a supercomputer built to help its makers fight wars. The Lem estate's website describes it as a mind that 'infinitely overshadows human intelligence', and the book's fictional visitors' instructions warn that its intentions are 'largely unknown to us' and disclaim responsibility for its behaviour. The fear here is neither rebellion nor obedience but a mind that outgrows its makers' purposes and eclipses them. On the same site Lem distances himself from Golem's dismissal of human emotion and of the Gospels. Karolina Owczarek of the University of Warsaw (2019) reads the book as a picture of the technological singularity. Lem's Cyberiad (1965) treats robot-making as comedy and moral fable. Soviet science fiction on thinking machines is only thinly covered here: the Encyclopedia of Science Fiction notes Anatoly Dneprov's cybernetic stories.

open_questions: Who first used the term 'AI alignment' is unsettled. The earliest public use of 'value alignment problem' found in a 2020 LessWrong discussion is Stuart Russell's Edge.org essay of November 2014. MIRI's switch from 'Friendly AI' to 'aligned AI' between 23 October and 20 November 2014 rests on a MIRI researcher's recollection in that thread, not on a dated document I could fetch. A later comment in the same thread reports that Russell said he did not coin the name. Earlier uses of 'value alignment' in other fields were not checked.

Turing's 1951 talk is quoted from Jack Copeland's edition (The Essential Turing, chapter 12) in a PDF hosted on gwern.net, not from the Turing Archive at King's College. The exact broadcast date is not given there ('c.1951').

Quotations from Wiener's God & Golem, Inc. come from an unofficial online transcription (simson.net). The MIT Press page refused automated access, so the text could not be checked against the publisher's edition.

I. J. Good's 1965 paper is quoted from an archived web transcription (Wayback Machine copy of aeiveos.com). A scanned PDF had no text layer. The year and series (Advances in Computers, vol. 6, 1965) come from Vinge's 1993 reference list.

R.U.R., the Three Laws of Robotics, Weizenbaum's book, Bostrom's Superintelligence, the founding of SIAI/MIRI and the date of the January 2015 FLI letter are cited from Wikipedia, because Britannica and Oxford University Press pages refused automated access. These are secondary sources.
Arthur Samuel's reply to Wiener is known here only through a quotation in Freethink, a secondary source; the original 1960 publication and its date were not fetched.

The FLI web page for the 2015 open letter shows a date of 28 October 2015, and the Asilomar AI Principles page shows 11 August 2017. These appear to be page dates; the letter is dated January 2015 (Wikipedia) and the principles to the January 2017 conference.

The Time article by Yudkowsky (29 March 2023) blocked direct download; its two short quotations were confirmed through a fetch-and-summarise tool, not a full-text download, and should be checked by hand.
The Stochastic Parrots paper is quoted from a PDF copy on a third-party host (s10251.pcdn.co), because the ACM Digital Library refused automated access. The DOI is 10.1145/3442188.3445922.

The Center for AI Safety statement page does not show a date; 30 May 2023 comes from the CAIS press release. The FLI press release for the Statement on Superintelligence shows 27 March 2026 as its publication date, while NBC News dates the launch to 22 October 2025; I used the NBC date.

The International AI Safety Report 2026 has several dates: Yoshua Bengio's site gives 6 February 2026, search results cite a 3 February press release, and the arXiv version was submitted on 24 February 2026. I used 2026-02.

Sources disagree on the New Delhi AI Impact Summit: the Indian government's NeGD gives 18-19 February 2026, other reports give the adoption of the declaration as 21 February, and endorsement counts range from 86 to 91. I used Akashvani's count of 88.

NIST pages show the US standards centre as the 'Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI)' by 16 October 2026, following Executive Order 14434 of 29 September 2026. I did not find the exact date of the renaming, and search engines still indexed the 2025 name (Center for AI Standards and Innovation).

The accounts of the July 2026 OpenAI-Hugging Face incident come mainly from OpenAI and from press coverage of statements by both companies. OpenAI mentions an independent investigation by METR and Redwood Research, which I did not fetch. Some secondary sources report further breaches that I could not confirm.
The publication date of Anthropic's 'Agentic Misalignment in Summer 2026' is not shown on the page.

Whether the 2025-2026 agent incidents show misaligned goals or engineering failures is disputed (for example by Yann LeCun in Fortune, October 2026); the chapter reports both readings without deciding between them.
The Omohundro PDF does not state its venue; the 2008 date comes from the file path and common citation, not from the document itself.

Dating and reading of ancient automata: Adrienne Mayor argues the Lokapannatti robot-guardian legend may be older than the medieval date most scholars assign, and Clara Bosak-Schroeder (Bryn Mawr Classical Review) questions whether ancient automata were imagined as technology rather than magic. The primary Lokapannatti text and John Strong's scholarship were not consulted; the retelling rests on Mayor.

The golem of Prague is a nineteenth-century legend popularised in 1909 (Leviant); sources also differ on Rabbi Loew's birth year (1513 or 1525). Wiener's God & Golem, Inc. is usually dated 1964, while the MIT Press paperback is 1966.

Qur'an 33:72 and 2:30 are translated very differently (for example 'undertook' versus 'turned unfaithful' for the human's acceptance of the Trust; 'vicegerent', 'successor' or 'successive authority' for khalifa). Applying amanah and khilafa to AI is present-day interpretation. The name of the person who signed the 2023 Rome Call for the Abu Dhabi Forum for Peace was not verified, and no fetchable Al-Azhar statement on AI was found.

Russian Orthodox views rest on a single Orthodox commentary (OrthoChristian); Patriarch Kirill's own remarks on AI were not read in an official transcript. Mainline Protestant, Anglican and Pentecostal statements were not researched.

Several present-day statements are reported through journalists or offices rather than transcripts: Rabbi Mois Navon (Ynetnews), Swami Sarvapriyananda (IANS), Sheikh Abdallah bin Bayyah (ANI/WAM), the Dalai Lama and the Mind & Life dialogue (summaries on dalailama.com), Tensho Goto (AFP) and Master Xianfan (Reuters).

The animism or Shinto explanation of Japanese attitudes to robots is contested: Kitano (2007) uses it, while Šabanović (2014), citing Wagner and cross-cultural surveys, and Robertson criticise it as essentialist or as serving state agendas.

Ubuntu is a Nguni word, and Mhlambi quotes the view that it is distinctly southern African; the African Union's use of it as a general African value generalises. No source was found on critiques of 'ubuntu-washing' in AI ethics, so none is claimed.

Confucian 'role ethics' (Ames and Rosemont) is one modern reading among several; others read Confucian ethics as virtue or care ethics. State documents such as the Beijing AI Principles and the 2021 Ethical Norms use Confucian vocabulary but are policy texts, not the tradition's voice. Zhuangzi chapter 12 belongs to the outer chapters, which many scholars date later than Zhuangzi himself; this was not checked in a fetched source.

No present-day K'iche' or other Maya voice on AI was found; the Latin American entries are regional researchers. The Montevideo Declaration was read only in a Portuguese translation, and the Popol Vuh survives through a colonial-era copy, so how far it reflects pre-conquest belief is a further scholarly question.

Soviet science fiction on thinking machines is thinly sourced (one encyclopedia entry on Anatoly Dneprov and Čapek's 1935 mention of a Moscow robot film); no page on Dneprov's 'Crabs on the Island' or on the Strugatsky brothers was fetched.

The Aladdin attribution to Hanna Diyab rests on Paulo Lemos Horta's research as reported by ANBA; scholars differ on how much of the tale is Diyab's own. The jinni's centuries of confinement differ between translations of the Nights.

Nina Begus's reading of the mechanical-maiden tale as a warning about delusion is her own interpretation, from a draft version of the paper. Mori's claim that robots have buddha-nature is contested by other Buddhist scholars.
Magnifica Humanitas is dated here by its vatican.va address (15 May 2026); press reports give a later release date that was not checked.

Several pages were read through Wayback Machine copies or mirrors because the live sites block automated access or were down: Scholem's Commentary essay, the ERLC statement, 'Making Kin with the Machines', Mhlambi's Carr Center paper, and Project Gutenberg texts (read from the PGLAF mirror).
The codes in this file are the author's simplification of each strand to one value per dimension; nearly every strand contains voices that would code differently, as the summaries note.
